title: The Security Bug AI Tools Write Constantly
description: Why AI-generated database queries default to string interpolation — a real, common vulnerability, not an edge case — and how to catch it in review.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize SQL injection risk in AI-generated database query code
Explain why parameterized queries close this vulnerability while string interpolation doesn't

contentSections.body: You ask an AI tool to "write a function that looks up a user by username" and it hands you something that runs perfectly in your local tests. It also happens to let anyone who controls the `username` input read your entire user table, or worse. This isn't a rare failure mode — string-built queries are one of the most common things AI coding tools produce when asked for something simple and database-shaped, because it's also the most common pattern in the training data they learned from, including a lot of insecure tutorials.

The pattern to watch for: any place user input gets inserted directly into a query string — via f-strings, string concatenation, or `.format()` — rather than passed as a separate parameter.

```python
# What AI tools commonly produce first:
def get_user(username):
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'"
    return db.execute(query)
```

If `username` is attacker-controlled and equals `' OR '1'='1`, the resulting query becomes `SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '' OR '1'='1'` — a condition that's always true, returning every row in the table. This isn't a contrived example; it's the textbook first SQL injection anyone learns, and it's exactly the shape AI tools reach for by default unless the prompt is specific about how to handle the input.

contentSections.question: What's the security flaw here, and what's the actual fix?

options.label: SQL injection — username is interpolated directly into the query string
No error handling if the database call fails
The function should be async for better performance

feedback.sql-injection-fstring: Correct. Any value in `username` becomes part of the literal SQL the database executes. An input like `' OR '1'='1` turns the WHERE clause into something always-true, returning every row. The fix is a parameterized query: `db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s", (username,))` (exact placeholder syntax varies by driver) — the database driver handles escaping, and the value can never be interpreted as SQL syntax no matter what it contains.
feedback.missing-error-handling: Missing error handling would be a real code-quality issue in production, but it's not what makes this snippet actively dangerous. Even with perfect error handling, the injection risk remains untouched — fix the query construction first.
feedback.should-use-async: Performance and concurrency style are legitimate review topics elsewhere, but irrelevant to whether this function is safe to expose to untrusted input, which is the actual problem here.

contentSections.flawExplanation: String-built queries are dangerous specifically because the database can't distinguish 'data the user typed' from 'SQL syntax' once they're concatenated into the same string — anything the attacker types becomes part of the command. Parameterized queries keep those two channels separate at the driver level, which is why they close the vulnerability entirely rather than just making it harder to exploit.

contentSections.scenario:
You're reviewing a pull request full of AI-generated database code. Six lines build or run a query. Assume `db.execute(sql, params)` hands the values to the driver's own parameter binding.

```python
1. db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")
2. db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", (name,))
3. db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + str(user_id))
4. db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '%s'" % name)
5. db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM {table} WHERE active = %s", (True,))
6. db.execute("SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY name LIMIT %s", (limit,))
```
contentSections.question: Select every line where an input value can become part of the SQL command itself.

items.label: Line 1 — f-string around name
Line 2 — %s placeholder with a tuple
Line 3 — concatenating str(user_id)
Line 4 — %-formatting into the string
Line 5 — table name from a variable
Line 6 — LIMIT as a bound parameter

explanation.line1: The lesson's own example. Interpolation happens in Python, before the driver sees anything, so the driver receives one finished string and has no way to tell which characters came from `name`.
explanation.line2: Safe. The command text and the value travel separately; the driver binds `name` as data. A quote inside `name` stays a quote inside the data and never becomes SQL syntax.
explanation.line3: `str()` is a conversion, not an escape. Set `user_id` to the text `1 OR 1=1` and the query becomes `WHERE id = 1 OR 1=1`. A numeric position needs no quote character at all to be injected — which is why this one gets past reviewers who are scanning for quotes.
explanation.line4: `%` here is Python's string formatting, not a database placeholder, and the resemblance to line 2 is exactly what makes it dangerous. The substitution happens before `db.execute` is called, so this is line 1 wearing a different costume.
explanation.line5: The *value* is bound correctly, and the table name is not. Parameter binding covers values only — never table names, column names, or `ORDER BY` directions. If `table` can be influenced by input, this is injectable. Identifiers have to come from a fixed allowlist you wrote by hand.
explanation.line6: Safe from injection — `limit` is bound as a value like any other. Some drivers will not accept a parameter in a `LIMIT` clause, so this may need rewriting for compatibility, but that is a separate question from whether it is exploitable.

contentSections.synthesis: The review question is never 'does this look escaped'. It is: did the value get concatenated into the command text before the driver saw it? Every unsafe line above answers yes, whether the joining was done by an f-string, a `+`, or a `%`. And parameter binding, where it does apply, applies only to values — identifiers are your problem to constrain in code.

contentSections.question: Why did the escaping fix leave the second function wide open?

options.label: The id sits outside any quotes, so there is nothing for quote-escaping to do
The escape is wrong — it should use a backslash, not a doubled quote
The only real problem is the missing int() conversion on order_id

feedback.no-quotes-needed: Correct. `WHERE id = {order_id}` places the value in a bare numeric position, so an attacker never needs a quote character. `1 OR 1=1` is already valid SQL there. The escape in `get_user` addressed one character in one context and, worse, left the team believing injection is a quoting problem.
feedback.escape-wrong-char: Doubling the quote is the correct escape for a standard SQL string literal — backslash escaping is driver- and mode-specific and is the less portable choice. The escape in `get_user` is not wrong. It is simply irrelevant to `get_order`, where no quote appears anywhere.
feedback.missing-int-cast: `int(order_id)` would stop this specific attack, and validating input types is a reasonable habit. But it is a patch at one call site: the next function someone writes will interpolate a string value, and the hole reopens. Binding parameters removes the whole class instead of this one instance.

contentSections.mechanism:
Injection is not a quoting problem, it is a channel problem. Once a value is concatenated into the command text, the database receives a single string and has to decide for itself which characters are data and which are syntax — and the attacker's characters get a vote in that decision.

Escaping tries to neutralise the characters that matter *in one context*. There is always another context: a bare numeric field where no quotes are needed, an identifier position, a `LIKE` pattern, a comment sequence. Each one needs its own escaping rule, and getting all of them right forever is not a thing review can guarantee.

Parameter binding sends the command and the values over separate channels. The value is never parsed as SQL, so what it contains stops being a question anyone has to answer.

contentSections.question: You found an interpolated query in an AI-generated pull request. Put the steps to close it out in order.
steps: Search the whole file for every other query built from an input value
Rewrite each one as a parameterized query using the driver's placeholder
Move any table or column name into a fixed allowlist in code
Run the existing tests to confirm normal inputs still behave the same
Add a test that passes ' OR '1'='1 as input and expects no rows
Search the rest of the codebase for the same interpolation pattern
contentSections.explanation:
Find them all before fixing one. A tool that produced this pattern once in a file almost always produced it several times, and fixing them in a single pass is far cheaper than three rounds of review.

Parameterize before writing tests. A test written against the broken version tends to encode the broken behaviour, and then you are debugging your test.

Identifiers come after values because parameter binding never covers them — this is the step that is easy to declare done too early, having fixed the `WHERE` clause and left the interpolated table name in place.

Existing tests first, then the new one: the existing suite tells you ordinary lookups still work, and the injection test is what actually proves the fix. Keep it — it fails against the old code, which is precisely what makes it worth its place in the suite.

The codebase-wide search goes last because by then you know the exact string to search for.

contentSections.body: When reviewing AI-generated code that touches a database, check query construction first, before anything else — string interpolation into a query is common enough in AI output that it's worth a dedicated pass, not just a general read-through.

title: When AI Silently Drops a Requirement
description: A working, well-written function that quietly fails to do the one thing it was actually asked to do — and why that's a harder bug to catch than a crash.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when AI-generated code satisfies the letter of a request while missing its actual intent
Verify order-sensitive requirements with a concrete example rather than assuming a plausible-looking implementation is correct

contentSections.body: You ask an AI tool to "remove duplicates from this list, keeping the original order." It hands back a one-liner that looks clean, runs without error, and returns the right *set* of items. You skim it, it looks fine, you move on. Three weeks later a user reports that their recently-viewed items are showing in a random order instead of most-recent-first — because the "remove duplicates" function never actually preserved order at all, it just happened to return items that were technically deduplicated.

This is a harder category of bug to catch than a crash or an obvious wrong answer, because the code runs and the *output is a valid answer to a slightly different question* than the one that was actually asked. The tell: whenever a requirement includes a word like "order," "preserve," "first," or "most recent," check whether the implementation actually has any mechanism for tracking that — or whether it silently dropped that half of the requirement in favor of an easier, unordered approach.

A very common shortcut AI tools reach for when asked to deduplicate: converting to a set and back. Sets are excellent for uniqueness. They are not ordered, and converting one back to a list does not restore the original sequence — it returns whatever order the set's internal structure happens to produce, which is unrelated to input order.

contentSections.question: Does this function satisfy the actual request?

options.label: No — it correctly removes duplicates but does not preserve order
Yes — Python sets preserve insertion order like dicts do
Yes, close enough — minor reordering doesn't matter for deduplication

feedback.no-loses-order: Correct. Run it and check: `list(set(['banana','apple','cherry','apple','date','banana']))` does not come back as `['banana','apple','cherry','date']` — it comes back reordered, because a set's iteration order depends on hashing, not insertion sequence. The function does half the job (uniqueness) and silently drops the other half (order) that was explicitly requested.
feedback.yes-sets-preserve-order: This is a common but incorrect assumption carried over from Python dicts, which have guaranteed insertion order since 3.7. Sets never got that guarantee — their iteration order is implementation-dependent on hashing, not insertion sequence. Try it against a real list rather than trusting the assumption.
feedback.yes-close-enough: Order was an explicit, stated part of the request, not an incidental detail — 'close enough' isn't a standard to review code against when the spec was specific. In a real product, this exact gap is what caused a user-visible bug (recently-viewed items showing in the wrong order).

contentSections.concept: The fix, when order genuinely needs preserving: `list(dict.fromkeys(items))` — using a dict (which does preserve insertion order) purely for its deduplication side effect, then converting the keys back to a list. Whenever you review code against a multi-part requirement, check each part separately against a concrete example rather than trusting that a clean-looking implementation covers all of it.

contentSections.question: Same failure shape, different language. Which part of the stated request did this code drop?

options.label: The comparator sorts oldest-first, so it returns the oldest emails
Spreading a Set discards the order, the way Python's set does
slice(0, limit) returns one item fewer than limit

feedback.sorts-oldest-first: Correct. `a.signupDate - b.signupDate` is ascending — oldest first. Every other line does its job, which is what makes this hard to see: you get a correct-looking list of unique emails that happens to be exactly backwards. `b.signupDate - a.signupDate` fixes the direction.
feedback.set-loses-order: This is the Python habit carried across languages, and it is worth un-learning deliberately. A JavaScript `Set` does preserve insertion order, so spreading it back into an array keeps the sequence it was given. That line is fine. The order was already inverted before the Set ever saw the data.
feedback.slice-off-by-one: `slice(0, 3)` returns three items — the end index is exclusive, so `(0, limit)` is the right way to take the first `limit` entries. The count is correct here; the order those entries were counted in is not.

contentSections.flawExplanation:
The same shape as the `dedupe` example above: most of a multi-part request satisfied, one part quietly inverted, nothing crashes.

There is a second dropped requirement in this function that nobody stated out loud. `users.sort(...)` sorts in place, so calling `recentUniqueEmails(roster, 3)` reorders `roster` for everyone else holding a reference to it. `[...users].sort(...)` avoids it.

Two different review questions catch the two bugs. Checking each stated part against a concrete input catches the reversed order. Asking 'did this change anything it was not asked to change' catches the mutation — and that one will never appear in the request, so it has to come from you.

contentSections.scenario: You put four requirements in one prompt. Back comes a short, clean function and a confident paragraph explaining it.
contentSections.question: Select every signal that genuinely suggests a requirement was dropped.

items.label: The requirement is about order, but nothing in the code tracks order
It uses a structure that discards the property you asked to keep
The explanation covers three of your four requirements and skips one
The function is much shorter than four requirements would suggest
The code has no comments
It uses a language feature you had not seen before

explanation.no-mechanism: The strongest signal on the list. If a property has to be preserved, something in the code has to carry it — an index, a list, an insertion-ordered structure, an explicit sort. No mechanism, no property, and you can check this without following the logic.
explanation.unordered-structure: `set` in the example above is exactly this. The requirement usually gets dropped at the point where a data structure was chosen, because the structure that drops it is the one that makes everything after it shorter.
explanation.explanation-silent: Worth reading the explanation for this alone. What a model does not claim to have done, it frequently has not done — and its own summary is a much faster read than the code.
explanation.shorter: Not proof by itself; some requirements genuinely collapse into one line. Treat it as a prompt to count: four requirements, one line, so which of the four does that line actually serve?
explanation.no-comments: Missing comments make review slower, but well-commented code drops requirements at the same rate as uncommented code — and an AI-written comment describes the intent, not what the line does. This tells you nothing about whether the requirement was met.
explanation.unfamiliar-syntax: Unfamiliar is not the same as wrong. `dict.fromkeys(items)` looks strange the first time and is the correct fix in this lesson. Look it up rather than treating novelty as a red flag; otherwise you spend your review attention on the code that is merely new to you.

contentSections.synthesis:
Every reliable signal here is a comparison between the request and the code. None of them are about how the code looks on its own.

That is the practical difference between reviewing AI output and reviewing a colleague's pull request. A colleague who did not implement your fourth requirement usually says so. A model produces a complete, confident, internally consistent answer to whichever version of the request it settled on — so the request has to be in front of you while you read.

contentSections.intro: Reviewing by eye is how the `dedupe` bug got through. Build a check you can actually run instead — four fields, and you can paste it into a REPL in under a minute.

fields.prompt: Which part of the request are you checking?

options.label: Preserves the original order
Returns a list

feedback.preserves the original order: Right — aim the check at the requirement the tool had a reason to skip. Uniqueness is what `set` optimises for and it comes free; order is the part that cost something, so it is the part that went missing.
feedback.returns a list: Almost anything the tool could write satisfies this, so a passing check teaches you nothing. Point the check at the expensive requirement, not the one that was never at risk.

fields.prompt: Which input would expose the problem?

options.label: Duplicates spread apart, order not alphabetical
Duplicates already adjacent, two values

feedback.['banana', 'apple', 'cherry', 'apple', ': Right — duplicates sit far apart, and first-seen order differs from alphabetical order, so a reordered result is obvious at a glance rather than needing to be worked out.
feedback.['apple', 'apple', 'banana', 'banana']: Two distinct values and adjacent duplicates leave only two possible orderings, so a broken implementation passes this roughly half the time. A test that passes by coincidence is worse than no test, because you stop looking.

fields.prompt: What is the expected output for that input?

options.label: First-seen order, duplicates removed
Alphabetical, duplicates removed

feedback.['banana', 'apple', 'cherry', 'date']: Right — 'keeping the original order' means first appearance wins. 'banana' appeared first in the input, so it stays first in the output, tidy or not.
feedback.['apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'date']: Alphabetical is a different requirement, and nobody asked for it. Writing the expected value from what the request said — before looking at what the code returns — is most of the value of doing this at all.

fields.prompt: How do you decide whether it passed?

options.label: Compare element by element, in order
options.value: compare the result to the expected list element by element, in order

options.label: Check both contain the same items
options.value: check that both lists contain the same items

fields.correctValue: compare the result to the expected list element by element, in order

feedback.compare the result to the expected list: Right — an order requirement can only be caught by an order-sensitive comparison. In Python, `==` between two lists already does exactly this.
feedback.check that both lists contain the same i: This is the one comparison the buggy version passes every time. An assertion that ignores order cannot detect that order was dropped — and that is how this bug ships to production with a green test suite around it.

contentSections.synthesis:
Requirement, input, expected output, comparison. Filling in all four never required reading the implementation once — and that is the point. A check written from the request tells you whether the code did what you asked. A check written from the code only tells you what the code already does, which you can find out by running it.

One of these per risky requirement, written before you look at the output, is what turns 'it looks fine' into something you actually know.

contentSections.body: The most dangerous AI-generated bugs aren't crashes — they're code that correctly answers a simpler question than the one actually asked. When a requirement has multiple parts, verify each part against a real example before trusting that a plausible-looking implementation covers all of them.

title: Off-by-one, inclusive bounds, and the fencepost that never dies
description: The single most common defect in generated code that runs without error and returns a wrong answer anyway — a boundary counted one item short or one item long.

learningObjectives.text: Identify off-by-one errors at loop bounds, slice boundaries, and inclusive date ranges
Convert an ambiguous 'first N' or 'last N' requirement into a concrete count to check an implementation against

contentSections.body:
You ask an AI tool for "the last 7 days of a user's login activity." It hands back:

```python
def last_n_days(logs, n=7):
    cutoff = date.today() - timedelta(days=n)
    return [log for log in logs if log.date >= cutoff]
```

It reads right. Run it locally and actually count what comes back: eight distinct calendar dates, not seven. `today - 7 days` lands exactly seven days before today, and the filter is `>=`, which keeps that boundary date *and* today itself — seven days back plus today is eight days on the calendar, not seven.

An off-by-one error is not a typo — it's a miscount at a boundary where the number of items between two ends depends on whether each end is included or excluded, and English descriptions of ranges are almost always ambiguous about that. "The last 7 days" could mean the 7 calendar dates ending today inclusive, or the 7 days strictly before today. Both are defensible readings of the same sentence, and only one of them is what `cutoff = today - timedelta(days=n)` combined with `>=` actually computes.

This is a specific, nameable failure mode, not a synonym for "any bug near an index." It shows up in four recurring shapes: loop bounds (`range(0, n)` yields `n` items, `range(1, n)` yields `n-1`), slice boundaries (`items[0:n]` versus `items[0:n+1]`), inclusive date or numeric ranges (exactly the login example above), and pagination math (page count computed from item count and page size). All four share the same root cause — the code has to decide whether an endpoint is a fencepost or a fence segment, and generated code picks one convention confidently without flagging that the English request was ambiguous about which one it meant.

contentSections.question: The requirement was "the last 7 days, inclusive of today." What's the actual defect?

options.label: `cutoff` is set n full days back, and the `>=` comparison then also keeps today — so the range spans n+1 calendar dates, not n
`date.today()` uses server local time instead of the user's timezone
The comparison should be `>` instead of `>=`, since `>=` is always wrong for date filtering

feedback.off-by-one-inclusive: Correct. To get exactly n calendar dates ending today inclusive, the cutoff needs to be `n - 1` days back, not `n` days back — `today - timedelta(days=n-1)` combined with `>=` gives exactly n dates. The bug isn't the operator, it's that the operator and the offset were chosen independently without anyone checking they agree on where the boundary actually falls.
feedback.timezone-mismatch: A real and separate concern for any date-boundary code running across timezones — but it's not what's making this specific function return eight dates instead of seven when tested against a single, fixed clock. Don't let a real-but-irrelevant issue substitute for actually counting the output.
feedback.wrong-comparison-operator: `>=` isn't inherently wrong for an inclusive range — it's the correct operator for the stated requirement (today included). The mistake is in how far back `cutoff` was set relative to that operator, not in the choice of operator itself.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Inclusive of today" and `>=` are actually consistent with each other — the sentence and the operator agree. What doesn't agree is the offset: subtracting a full `n` days for an n-day *inclusive* window overshoots by exactly one, the way it always does when an inclusive count and an exclusive subtraction are mixed without adjustment. This is the fencepost problem in its purest form: n days of fence needs n-1 gaps between them, not n.

contentSections.body: Before trusting any "first N" or "last N" implementation, write down the concrete list of items it should return for a small N you can count by hand, and check the code against that list — not against the sentence.

The same miscount recurs across contexts that don't look related at first glance. A generated retry helper `for attempt in range(max_retries):` makes exactly `max_retries` attempts total — a comment reading "retries 3 times, so 4 attempts including the first" describes a *different* function than the one written, and nobody will notice until an integration that genuinely needs 4 attempts gets 3. A generated pagination helper computing `total_pages = total_items // page_size` silently drops a final partial page — 101 items at 20 per page reports 5 pages instead of 6, and the 101st item is unreachable through the UI. Both are the exact same failure as the login-activity example: a count derived from a boundary, where the boundary math quietly picked exclusive when the requirement meant inclusive, or vice versa.

The practical defense is cheap and doesn't require reading the implementation carefully: pick a small, concrete case where you can count the right answer by hand — 3 items, a 2-day window, a 21-item list at page size 20 — and check the function's actual output against that count. A boundary bug that survives a careful reading of the code almost never survives being run against a hand-counted case, because the miscount is invisible in prose and glaring in a concrete example.

contentSections.scenario: A generated `business_days_between(start, end)` function is meant to answer: for a Monday `start` and the Friday of that same week as `end`, how many business days does "Monday through Friday, inclusive of both ends" cover?
contentSections.question: Predict the count a correct implementation should return for this Monday-to-Friday, both-ends-included range.
contentSections.explanation: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday — five inclusive days. The generated implementation you'll usually see for this is `(end - start).days`, which computes the *gap* between the two dates (4) rather than the *count of days spanned* (5) — a difference-of-dates calculation silently substituted for a count-of-days-inclusive requirement. The fix is `(end - start).days + 1` whenever both endpoints are meant to be included, which is exactly the same fencepost adjustment as the login-activity example, just spelled differently.

contentSections.body: A difference between two dates or indices is a gap, not a count — an inclusive count of items spanning that gap is always the gap plus one, and generated code frequently returns the gap.

title: Copy-paste symmetry errors the eye slides over
description: Code that handles two parallel cases — width and height, min and max, x and y — where one branch was copied from the other and one reference inside it wasn't updated to match.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize symmetric code structures (paired axes, paired bounds, paired branches) as a specific risk site for an un-updated copy
Check a symmetric pair of code blocks by verifying every reference in the second block was actually swapped, not just structurally mirrored

contentSections.title: The variable that didn't get the memo

contentSections.body:
This is a distinct failure mode from a typo: the code isn't randomly wrong, it's wrong in a way that mirrors a correct structure closely enough that a fast read matches the *shape* and moves on. Two blocks that are meant to be parallel — one per axis, one per bound, one per branch of an if/else — are extremely cheap to produce by copying the first block and editing it, and that's very close to how a model actually generates the second block: conditioned heavily on the pattern of the first, with a much weaker signal pulling every individual token toward being correctly re-targeted.

The result is a defect that survives structural review specifically because the structure is right. Counting the `if` statements, counting the error messages, checking that both branches exist — none of that catches a variable that's syntactically valid, semantically plausible (`max_width` is a real variable in scope, of a compatible type), and simply the wrong one. The eye slides over it because everything nearby is correct: right number of branches, right general shape, right *kind* of variable in that position — just not the one that belongs there.

This shows up anywhere a codebase has a genuinely symmetric structure: width/height, min/max, x/y, left/right, source/destination, old/new. Any pair like that is a place where one half was very plausibly copied from the other, and copying is exactly the operation that leaves stale references behind.

contentSections.question: What's the actual defect, and why would a fast read of this function miss it?

options.label: The second `if` compares `height` against `max_width` instead of `max_height` — so an over-height, in-bounds-width image is never rejected
The error message on the second line references `max_height` while the comparison uses a different variable, which is just a cosmetic inconsistency
The function doesn't check for negative width or height values, which is the more serious gap

feedback.wrong-var-height-check: Correct. The comparison `height > max_width` will almost never fire correctly — a tall, narrow image can sail through with a height far beyond `max_height`, as long as it stays under `max_width`, because `max_height` is never actually compared against anything in this function.
feedback.error-message-mismatch: The error message referencing `max_height` isn't a separate cosmetic bug — it's the tell. The message was clearly written for the correct comparison (`height` vs `max_height`), which is strong evidence the comparison itself is the thing that regressed, not the message.
feedback.missing-negative-check: A real gap in a lot of validators, and worth raising separately — but it's not the defect actually present and exploitable in this specific snippet, and calling it out instead of the variable mismatch means the one-line fix that actually matters here gets missed.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Both `if` blocks have the identical two-line shape, the identical general logic (compare a dimension to its limit, raise with a formatted message), and even a message that mentions the right variable — everything a shape-level read would check lines up. The single reference that didn't get updated when the height block was copied from the width block is `max_width` on the comparison line, and it's the only thing standing between this function working and silently approving any image, however tall, that happens to be narrow enough.

contentSections.body: When you see a symmetric pair of code blocks, don't just check that the second block exists and has the same shape — check that every single reference inside it was actually re-targeted to the second case, one at a time.

Reading symmetric pairs one at a time doesn't scale to a real review — a generated module can have a dozen paired axes, bounds, or branches, and reading each pair carefully for twenty minutes isn't realistic inside a normal review pass. Two techniques compress the check without losing it.

First: search, don't read. If a function has a `width`/`height` or `min`/`max` pair, grep the second block specifically for any occurrence of the *first* case's variable name. A correctly mirrored block should contain zero references to the other case's names — any hit is either a genuine cross-reference (rare, and worth understanding on its own) or exactly this bug.

Second: diff the two blocks against each other, not against your memory of what they should say. Copy the first block, mechanically substitute every occurrence of the first-case name with the second-case name, and diff the result against what the code actually contains. Anywhere the diff shows a line that *should* have changed and didn't is the defect — this turns a read-and-judge task into a read-and-compare task, which is far more reliable under review fatigue, and it's the same principle as the earlier module's habit of computing a baseline before reading an assertion: you're generating the expected value independently, then comparing, rather than reading the actual value and asking whether it feels right.

contentSections.question: Select every line where a symmetry-copy error actually changes the function's behavior, not just its wording.

items.label: Line 2 (`if end_date < min_date`) — compares `end_date` against `min_date`, which is the intended check for a too-early end date
The message on line 2 ("end_date after max_date") describes the wrong condition — it should say 'before min_date', matching what's actually being checked
Line 4 (`if end_date > max_date`) — correctly checks `end_date` against `max_date`, matching both its comparison and its message
Line 1 (`if start_date < min_date`) — comparison and message both correctly describe the same condition

explanation.line2: The comparison itself (`end_date < min_date`) is exactly the check this line needs to perform — an end date earlier than the allowed minimum is a real validation failure, and this line catches it correctly.
explanation.msg2: This is the actual defect: the comparison logic is right, but the error message was copied from line 4 (or written for the wrong case) and describes a completely different condition. Anyone debugging a rejected request from this message will look for the wrong cause, since the message and the real reason for rejection don't match.
explanation.line4: Comparison and message agree with each other and with the intended check — nothing to flag here.
explanation.line1: Comparison and message agree — this is the correctly-written first half of the pair that the rest should have been copied from accurately.

contentSections.synthesis: This one inverts the usual pattern: the comparison logic on line 2 is actually correct, and it's the *message* that's the stale copy, silently describing the wrong condition. The lesson generalizes past 'the comparison is wrong' — anything that was copied and could plausibly diverge (a comparison, a message, a variable passed to a downstream call) is a candidate, and each has to be checked on its own rather than assuming that because the logic is right, everything nearby copied from it is too.

contentSections.body: Symmetry bugs aren't limited to comparison operators — an error message, a log line, or a downstream function call can just as easily be the thing that got copied without being re-targeted.

title: Plausible defaults that are wrong for your system
description: A default value that's a completely reasonable choice in general — a timeout, a page size, a currency, a timezone — and specifically wrong for the system it just got written into.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a default value in generated code as an unstated assumption about the calling system, not a neutral technical choice
Check a generated default against the specific system's actual constraints rather than against whether the default is reasonable in isolation

contentSections.body:
A default is a claim about the environment the code will run in, made silently, by whoever or whatever wrote the function — and a generated default is drawn from the statistical center of a huge number of other codebases' defaults, not from anything about *this* system. `timeout=30` is genuinely a fine default for a general-purpose library used by unknown callers in unknown environments; that's exactly the population an AI tool's training data is disproportionately drawn from. It is a specific, checkable fact about your system whether 30 seconds is safe, and the model has no access to that fact — it can only produce the value that's typical across everywhere else.

The same shape recurs across every default a generated function reaches for: a page size (`limit=100` when your database's connection pool chokes above 20 concurrent large result sets), a currency (`amount: float` defaulting to a bare number when your system needs every amount tagged with a currency code because it operates in six countries), a character encoding (`open(path)` defaulting to the platform's locale encoding instead of UTF-8, fine on the author's machine and wrong on a server with a different locale), a retry count, a cache TTL, a batch size. None of these defaults are wrong in the abstract — each is a defensible choice for *some* system. The question a review has to ask isn't "is this a reasonable default" but "is this a reasonable default for the specific system this code is about to run inside."

contentSections.scenario:
A generated CSV export function:

```python
def export_report(rows, path):
    with open(path, 'w') as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerows(rows)
```

It works perfectly in every test run on the developer's laptop. Deployed to a Linux server with a minimal locale configuration, exported reports containing customer names with accented characters (é, ñ, ü) come out corrupted or raise `UnicodeEncodeError`.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind code that works on one machine and fails on another with the exact same input?

options.label: `open(path, 'w')` without an explicit `encoding=` argument uses the operating system's default locale encoding, which is UTF-8 on the developer's machine and something narrower (often ASCII-compatible only) on the minimal server locale
Python's `csv` module doesn't support non-ASCII characters at all, on any platform
The server's disk or filesystem is corrupting the file during the write

feedback.locale-dependent-encoding: Correct. `open()` with no `encoding` argument delegates to `locale.getpreferredencoding()`, which reads the operating system's configured locale — this is genuinely UTF-8 on most modern developer laptops and genuinely something narrower on many minimal server images, which is exactly why the same unmodified code behaves differently on the two machines with the identical input.
feedback.csv-module-broken: The `csv` module itself is encoding-agnostic — it writes whatever bytes the underlying file object accepts. The module isn't the problem; the file object's encoding, silently inherited from the machine's locale, is.
feedback.server-corrupted-file: Nothing about this failure pattern — consistent, reproducible corruption specifically on non-ASCII characters, on one machine and not another — looks like disk corruption, which would be random and not systematically tied to character encoding.

contentSections.mechanism: A default that's silently sourced from the operating system rather than stated explicitly in the code is a default that travels with the machine, not with the code — it means the exact same source file has different real behavior on different deployment targets, invisible in any code review that only reads the source and doesn't know each environment's locale configuration. The fix, `open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8')`, doesn't just fix the bug — it converts an implicit, environment-dependent default into an explicit, portable one, which is the general shape of the fix for this whole category: name the assumption in the code instead of letting the platform supply it silently.

contentSections.body: When you see a default value in generated code, ask what specific fact about your system would make it wrong — a gateway timeout, a connection pool size, a locale, a currency — before asking whether the value itself looks reasonable.

contentSections.title: Where these live in your system

contentSections.body:
Plausible-but-wrong defaults cluster at a predictable set of locations, which makes them checkable without auditing every literal in a diff. Anything crossing a network boundary carries timeout, retry, and payload-size defaults that depend on what's on the other end of that specific connection — your gateway, your downstream service's actual latency, your load balancer's own limits. Anything touching money carries currency, rounding-mode, and precision defaults that depend on which currencies and which accounting rules your system actually has to support. Anything touching dates or times carries timezone defaults that depend on where your users and your servers actually are, which are very often not the same place. Anything reading or writing files or network bytes carries encoding defaults that depend on your specific deployment target's locale, as just seen.

The review habit that catches this category reliably: for every default value in a diff touching one of these four boundaries — network, money, time, encoding — ask "what's the actual constraint here, and does this number happen to satisfy it, or does it just happen to be a common choice." A default chosen to satisfy a real constraint you can name ("11 seconds because the gateway kills at 11") is trustworthy. A default that's merely common ("30 seconds because that's what most examples use") needs the actual constraint looked up before it can be trusted, and looking it up is usually a two-minute check against a config file or a runbook, not a research project.

contentSections.scenario: A generated batch-processing job includes several default values. Assume the system in question processes financial transactions across the US, UK, and Eurozone, running on a managed database with a hard connection limit of 20.
contentSections.question: Select every default here that's a real risk specifically for this system, not just a generic "could theoretically be wrong somewhere" concern.

items.label: `batch_size=500` rows fetched per query, on a connection pool capped at 20 concurrent connections
`amount: float` with no currency field, for a system that processes transactions in three different currencies
`log_level='INFO'` as the default verbosity for the job's internal logger
`max_retries=3` with no backoff, for calls to a downstream payment processor with a documented rate limit

explanation.batch-size-500: Not inherently dangerous in isolation, but worth checking against the specific constraint stated: a large `batch_size` increases per-query memory and lock duration, and whether 500 rows is safe depends on the actual row width and the actual connection pool pressure — this is a 'go check the real number' case, not an automatic pass or fail.
explanation.amount-float: A genuine defect risk for this specific system: a system explicitly stated to run across three currencies needs every monetary amount tagged with which currency it's in, or arithmetic and comparisons across records silently mix USD, GBP, and EUR values as if they were the same unit.
explanation.log-level-info: Log verbosity doesn't touch correctness, money, or an external constraint — it's a genuinely low-stakes default that doesn't need the same scrutiny as the others, even though it's technically also 'a default value in the diff.'
explanation.retry-3: A real risk given the stated fact: retrying against a rate-limited processor without backoff can itself trigger or worsen a rate-limit response, turning a transient failure into a cascading one — the retry count isn't the problem on its own, the missing backoff against a documented rate limit is.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the three real risks: each one is dangerous specifically because of a fact stated about *this* system — the connection limit, the multi-currency requirement, the documented rate limit — not because the default is unusual or bad practice in general. The log-level default is the control case: it's also a default value sitting right there in the diff, and it's genuinely fine, because nothing about this system's stated constraints makes it dangerous. Scrutiny has to be aimed by the system's real constraints, not spent evenly across every literal in sight.

contentSections.body: A default is wrong relative to a system, not in the abstract — the fix isn't memorizing which numbers are bad, it's checking each default's boundary (network, money, time, encoding) against what you actually know about your own system.

title: The happy path implemented perfectly and nothing else
description: A function that does exactly what a working, correct call to it should do — and nothing at all for the empty list, the missing field, the failed dependency, or the concurrent caller.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish code that's wrong from code that's correct but incomplete — implemented only for inputs that succeed
Generate the specific non-happy-path cases a function needs to handle from its own signature and the domain it operates in

contentSections.title: Correct is not the same as complete

contentSections.body:
A generated checkout total calculator:

```python
def calculate_total(items):
    subtotal = sum(item.price * item.quantity for item in items)
    tax = subtotal * 0.08
    return subtotal + tax
```

Every test with a real cart passes. Every demo works. It ships. Three weeks later, a customer removes every item from their cart on the review page without navigating away, and the "proceed to payment" button — which calls this function on an empty list — charges them $0.00 and the order confirms, because `sum()` on an empty generator is `0`, `0 * 0.08` is `0`, and nothing in this function was ever asked what an empty cart should do, so it does the only thing it was ever written to do: the arithmetic.

This is a different failure mode from the ones already covered — it isn't a miscount, a stale reference, or a wrong constant. The code is a completely correct implementation of a real subset of the requirement: the case where the input is well-formed and everything downstream behaves. What's missing isn't inside the function; it's the cases the function was never asked to consider, because the prompt (and the training data behind the model's default behavior) both concentrate overwhelmingly on the working scenario. A tutorial, a documentation example, and a Stack Overflow answer almost all show the happy path — showing an empty-cart edge case would make the example longer and less clear for the thing it's actually trying to teach, so that case just isn't there in the material the pattern comes from.

The practical tell is structural, not behavioral: a function this size with zero conditionals, zero guard clauses, and zero exception handling, operating in a domain (checkout, in this case) that obviously has failure and edge cases, is a function that was written for the one path where nothing needs to be decided. That absence is informative on its own, before you've even thought about which specific edge case might be missing — a checkout function with no branches at all is a checkout function that hasn't met an edge case yet.

contentSections.scenario:
A generated function fetches a user's most recent order:

```python
def get_latest_order(user_id):
    orders = db.query(Order).filter_by(user_id=user_id).all()
    return sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o.created_at)[-1]
```
contentSections.question: What happens when this runs for a user_id with zero orders in the database — a brand new signup, for example?

options.label: `sorted([])[-1]` raises an `IndexError: list index out of range` — the function crashes rather than returning something like `None`
It returns `None`, which is the sensible default for 'no orders exist'
It returns an empty `Order` object with default field values

feedback.index-error: Correct. `sorted([])` returns `[]`, and indexing an empty list with `[-1]` raises `IndexError`. Nowhere in this function is there a check for an empty `orders` list — it was written for, and only tested against, users who already have order history.
feedback.returns-none: This is what a version of this function that had actually considered the empty case might do — but nothing in the code as written returns `None` for anything. Don't credit the code with sensible behavior it doesn't actually contain.
feedback.returns-empty-order: There's no code path anywhere in this function that constructs an `Order` with default values — this answer describes a defensive pattern the function would need to opt into explicitly, not something that happens by default.

contentSections.concept: A function with no explicit handling for an empty collection doesn't have a hidden reasonable default — it has whatever happens to occur when the underlying operations (sorting, indexing, aggregating) are run on an empty input, and that's frequently a crash, not a graceful fallback. New user, first visit, empty cart, first-time API caller with no history: these are not rare edge cases, they're the very first interaction with the system for a meaningful fraction of real users, and "never yet used the feature" is often the single most common non-happy-path state a function will actually encounter in production.

contentSections.body: "Zero of something" — zero items, zero orders, zero matches — is usually the single most common non-happy-path state a function meets in production, not a rare edge case, because it's exactly what every brand-new user or empty collection looks like.

The missing cases aren't random — they're generatable from two sources without needing domain expertise you don't have. The first source is the function's own signature and body: every collection can be empty or have one element instead of many; every optional field can be missing; every external call (a database query, an API request) can fail, time out, or return something malformed; every number can be zero or negative even if the happy path only exercises positive ones. Reading the function once specifically to ask "what if this list is empty," "what if this call fails," "what if this field is null" generates a checklist mechanically, without needing to know anything about the business domain.

The second source is the domain the function operates in, which the first source can't see. A checkout function's domain-specific edge cases include an empty cart (covered), a cart where every item is now out of stock between page load and checkout, a price that changed while the cart sat open, a payment that partially succeeds. These aren't derivable from the function's types alone — `items: list[CartItem]` doesn't tell you stock levels can change concurrently — they come from knowing what checkout actually has to survive in the real world. A review that only checks the type-derivable cases (empty list, null field) catches real bugs but misses the domain-specific ones; a review that only thinks about domain scenarios but skips the mechanical type-derivable check misses the cheapest, most common gap. Both passes are needed, and the type-derivable one takes under a minute per function.

contentSections.question: Put these four checks in the order that generates the widest coverage per minute spent — mechanical, type-derivable checks first, before the checks that require domain knowledge and more thought per case.
steps: For every collection parameter, ask what happens if it's empty
For every optional or nullable field, ask what happens if it's missing
For every external call, ask what happens if it fails or returns something malformed
For the specific domain this function operates in, ask what real-world event between two calls to this function could invalidate an assumption it makes
contentSections.explanation: The first three checks are mechanical — they can be run against any function's signature and body in under a minute, without knowing anything about what the function is actually for, and they catch the empty-cart, missing-field, and failed-dependency shapes of this exact bug class. The fourth check requires actually knowing the domain — what can genuinely happen to a cart, an order, a user between two calls — and takes real thought per case, so it belongs last: run the cheap, mechanical checks first to catch the common structural gaps fast, then spend the more expensive domain-reasoning time on what's left. Doing it in the reverse order risks spending all the available review time on domain scenarios and never getting to the mechanical pass that would have caught the empty-cart bug in ten seconds.

contentSections.body: Generate the missing cases in two passes: a fast, mechanical pass over every collection, optional field, and external call in the function's own signature, then a slower domain-knowledge pass over what can actually happen in the real world between two calls to it.

title: Why these patterns recur: what the model learned from
description: The four patterns this module covers aren't random — they're the specific shape of what's overrepresented and underrepresented in the code a model was trained on, which makes them predictable rather than merely common.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why off-by-one, symmetry, wrong-default, and happy-path-only defects occur at a higher rate in generated code than in equivalent hand-written code
Use the training-data explanation to predict which category a new, unfamiliar generated function is most at risk from, based on what the function does

contentSections.title: The training data is mostly the happy path

contentSections.body: Every pattern in this module traces back to the same source: a model producing the statistically most likely continuation of code similar to what it's seen, and what it's seen is not a representative sample of production code — it's disproportionately tutorials, documentation examples, Stack Overflow answers, and open-source code that survived to be popular enough to be well-represented. All four of those sources share a bias: they optimize for teaching or demonstrating one concept clearly, and error handling, edge cases, and system-specific configuration make an example longer and muddier without teaching the concept any better. A tutorial on calculating a cart total teaches summing prices; it doesn't also want to teach empty-list handling in the same fifteen lines, so it doesn't include it — and a model trained heavily on material shaped like that reproduces the same shape by default.

This explains the happy-path pattern directly, but it also explains the other three less obviously. Off-by-one errors persist because boundary conventions are genuinely inconsistent across the training corpus — some languages and libraries are 0-indexed, some are 1-indexed, some ranges are inclusive, some exclusive — and a model has absorbed all of these conventions simultaneously without a reliable signal for which one applies to the specific boundary in front of it right now; it produces *a* plausible convention, not necessarily *the* correct one for this exact case. Copy-paste symmetry errors persist because the statistically likely way to generate a second, parallel block of code is heavily conditioned on the first block's tokens — which is exactly the mechanism that makes stale references likely, since the model is pattern-completing from the first block rather than independently reasoning about what the second block specifically needs. Plausible-but-wrong defaults persist because a default value is, by definition, the model's best guess at the *typical* case across everything it's seen — and "typical across a huge, generic corpus" is a different question from "correct for this one specific system," which the model has no visibility into at all.

The unifying idea: none of these four patterns are random noise. Each is the predictable output of optimizing for "plausible across many contexts" applied to a task that actually needed "correct for this one specific context." That's not a flaw that better prompting fully removes — it's a structural gap between what the training process rewards and what any single deployment needs, which is exactly why review, not better prompting alone, is the durable fix.

contentSections.question: A generated function computes shipping cost by ZIP code distance band, with no error handling of any kind and a hardcoded `base_rate = 5.99`. Before reading further: which of this module's four patterns is this function most likely to be missing, based purely on what you already know about where generated code's gaps concentrate?
contentSections.answer: Most likely missing: happy-path-only handling (no branch for an unrecognized or malformed ZIP code) and a plausible-but-wrong default (a flat `base_rate` that doesn't account for whichever real shipping zones or carriers the actual system uses).
contentSections.hint: A function with zero conditionals operating in a domain (shipping, geography) that obviously has edge cases is the structural tell from the happy-path lesson — and a bare hardcoded rate is exactly the shape of default the earlier lesson flagged.

contentSections.body: These four patterns aren't a random assortment of things to remember — they're the predictable consequence of a model optimizing for 'plausible across many training examples' being applied to a task that needed 'correct for one specific system,' and that gap doesn't close with a better prompt alone.

contentSections.title: What this changes about how you review

contentSections.body:
Knowing the mechanism changes what you look for before you've read a single line. A function that crosses a boundary — a date range, a pagination cutoff, a loop count — is specifically at risk of the off-by-one pattern, because boundary conventions are exactly where the training corpus is genuinely inconsistent; that's worth a boundary-specific check even before the rest of the function is read. A function with a visibly symmetric structure — paired axes, paired branches, an obvious copy-then-edit shape — is specifically at risk of a stale reference, because that structure is exactly what the pattern-completion mechanism reproduces most faithfully. A function with any default value at all, at a network, money, time, or encoding boundary, is specifically at risk of a default that's typical-in-general and wrong-for-this-system. And a function with zero conditionals in a domain that obviously has edge cases is specifically at risk of being a happy-path-only implementation.

This doesn't replace reading the code — it directs where the reading effort goes first, which matters because review time is a real constraint, not an unlimited resource. A ten-line generated function with an obvious boundary calculation deserves the boundary check before anything else; a ten-line generated function with no boundaries, no symmetry, no defaults, and no domain edge cases genuinely needs less scrutiny than one that has all four risk shapes present at once. The next module builds directly on this: the same 'where does the training data's shape create a gap' reasoning applies to a much higher-stakes category — the places untrusted input reaches something that will execute it.

contentSections.scenario: Across a large, informal survey of AI-generated pull requests flagged in code review for a genuine correctness bug (not style), a significant share trace back to just these four patterns combined: off-by-one/boundary errors, copy-paste symmetry errors, wrong defaults, and happy-path-only implementations.
contentSections.question: Predict, as a rough percentage, how much of the correctness-bug share these four combined patterns plausibly account for, given how structurally common each one is.
contentSections.explanation: There's no single universally-cited number here, and the exact figure varies by study and by codebase — but practitioner reports and internal review audits at multiple organizations converge on a strikingly large share, commonly cited in the 50-70% range, being attributable to this small set of structural patterns rather than to novel, one-off logic errors. The number matters less than what it implies: a reviewer who has internalized checks for exactly these four shapes is covering the majority of what's actually likely to be wrong, for a small, fixed amount of review effort — which is the entire practical payoff of learning the mechanism instead of just memorizing four unrelated examples.

contentSections.body: Before reading a generated function's implementation, scan its signature and shape for which of the four risk patterns it's structurally exposed to — a boundary, a symmetric pair, a default, an edge-case-free domain — and spend your review attention there first.

title: Build your own defect-pattern checklist from real output
description: Generate real code from an AI tool for a task you actually need, find the defects it contains using this module's four patterns, and turn what you found into a checklist with a real example behind every entry.

learningObjectives.text: Apply all four of this module's defect patterns to genuinely AI-generated code, not curated examples
Produce a reusable review checklist grounded in real, specific defects you personally found

contentSections.body: Every example this module used was already found and written up for you. Real review doesn't come with the defect flagged in advance — it comes as a diff, and the defect is somewhere in it or it isn't. This lab closes that gap: generate genuinely new code from an AI tool for something you actually need, and find what's actually wrong with it, if anything, using exactly the four patterns from this module.

contentSections.title: Build a defect-pattern checklist from real generated output
contentSections.brief: Pick three to five small, distinct tasks you'd genuinely want AI-generated code for — a data-processing function, a validation helper, a small API handler, a report calculator, whatever fits something you're actually working on. Generate real code for each from an AI tool of your choice. Review each one specifically for this module's four patterns (off-by-one/boundary, copy-paste symmetry, plausible-but-wrong default, happy-path-only), plus anything else you notice. Not every piece of generated code will have a defect in every category, or any defect at all — that's a legitimate, useful finding too.
contentSections.deliverable: A checklist of at least eight defect-pattern entries, each with a real code excerpt you personally generated and caught, the category it belongs to, and the one-line fix. If your generated code turns out cleaner than expected, entries can include 'checked for X, not present, here's why' as a legitimate, documented negative result — a checklist that only ever records defects it found tells you nothing about how thorough the checking was.

stages.checkpoint: Every snippet has been checked against all four patterns explicitly, with a written result for each — not just an overall pass/fail impression.

rubric.meets: A defect entry names the actual code change that closes it; a clean-result entry explains what was specifically checked to be confident nothing's there.

contentSections.body: A checklist built from defects you personally found in code you personally generated is worth more than one copied from someone else's examples — it's calibrated to the kind of code you actually generate, and you already know exactly what each entry looks like in practice.

description: Ten questions, all from this module. Each course is sold separately, so nothing here draws on other courses. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's four defect patterns and why they recur, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — The Bugs AI Writes Most

questions.from: This module — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated 'last N days' filter subtracts N full days and then uses `>=` to include the boundary date. What's the general shape of this defect?

options.label: Mixing an inclusive requirement with an exclusive-style offset — the result spans N+1 dates instead of N
Using `>=` instead of `>`, which is always the wrong operator for date filtering
A timezone bug, since `date.today()` doesn't specify a timezone

questions.explanation: The offset (`n` full days back) and the inclusive comparison (`>=`, which also keeps today) don't agree with each other — together they span n+1 dates. The fix is adjusting the offset to `n-1`, not changing the operator, which is already correct for an inclusive requirement.

questions.from: This module — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: What's the structural tell that a symmetric pair of code blocks (like a width/height validator) might contain a stale, un-retargeted reference?

options.label: The second block's shape matches the first block's shape closely enough that a fast structural read confirms 'looks right' without checking every individual reference
The function uses more than two parameters
There's no reliable tell — this defect is genuinely undetectable without running the code

questions.explanation: The whole risk of this pattern is that the second block was very plausibly copied from the first, which reproduces the shape faithfully while leaving individual references weakly checked — a mechanical check (grep the second block for the first case's variable names, or diff against an independently constructed expected version) reliably catches it without needing to run anything.

questions.from: This module — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: Why is `timeout=30` a genuinely reasonable default in general and still worth checking specifically for your system?

options.label: Because 'reasonable in general' is a statement about the training data's typical case, and says nothing about a specific fact — like your API gateway's actual timeout — that could make it wrong here
Because 30 seconds is objectively too long for any HTTP call in any system
It isn't worth checking — a default that's reasonable in general is reasonable everywhere it's used

questions.explanation: The gateway-timeout example showed this precisely: 30 seconds is a defensible general-purpose default and specifically wrong against an 11-second gateway limit. The check isn't 'is this a bad number,' it's 'does this number satisfy a real constraint of this specific system' — network, money, time, and encoding boundaries are where that check pays off most.

questions.from: This module — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated checkout function has zero conditionals and operates on a list of cart items. What should that absence of branching make you check first?

options.label: What happens when the list is empty — the single most common non-happy-path state a function meets, since it's the state of every brand-new user or empty collection
Whether the function's variable names are descriptive enough
Whether the function is fast enough for a large cart

title: SQL injection: the bug generated database code writes by default
description: Why the default shape of a generated database query builds the exact channel that lets attacker-controlled text become part of the command itself — beyond the quoted-string case everyone already half-knows.

learningObjectives.text: Identify SQL injection in generated code beyond the quoted-string case, including numeric positions, identifiers, and ORM raw-query methods
Explain why the vulnerability is about the channel data travels through, not about which characters happen to be dangerous

contentSections.body:
You ask an AI tool to write an internal admin tool endpoint: "look up orders by the sort column the frontend requests." It hands back:

```python
def list_orders(sort_by, direction='ASC'):
    query = f"SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY {sort_by} {direction}"
    return db.execute(query)
```

Every request from the actual frontend passes `sort_by='created_at'` or `sort_by='total'` — values from a dropdown, never typed freely — so this looks completely safe in every test anyone runs against it. It's also directly exploitable: nothing stops a request from setting `sort_by` to `created_at; DROP TABLE orders; --`, and no quote character is anywhere in that payload, which is exactly what makes it invisible to a reviewer scanning for quotes.

The version of SQL injection most reviewers already recognize is the quoted-string case: `f"...WHERE name = '{name}'"`, where an attacker closes the quote early and appends their own SQL. That pattern is real and common, but treating it as *the* definition of SQL injection is exactly what lets the other shapes through. Injection is not about quotes — it's about whether attacker-influenced text was concatenated into the command string before the database driver ever saw it, regardless of whether that position in the query happens to need quotes.

Three shapes generated code reaches for constantly, none of which involve a quote character: a numeric or unquoted position (`WHERE id = {order_id}`, where a string like `1 OR 1=1` needs no quote to become valid SQL); an identifier position — a table name, column name, or `ORDER BY` direction, exactly like the `sort_by` example, where parameter binding *cannot help at all* even if you wanted to use it, because binding only ever substitutes values, never column or table names; and an ORM's own raw-query escape hatch (`Model.objects.raw(f"...")`, `db.session.execute(text(f"..."))`), which developers and AI tools alike reach for the moment a query gets slightly too complex for the ORM's query builder, and which is exactly as vulnerable as raw SQL the moment an f-string enters it.

contentSections.question: This function only ever receives `sort_by` values from a fixed frontend dropdown in every test anyone's run. Is it safe to ship?

options.label: No — `sort_by` and `direction` land in identifier/keyword positions that parameter binding can't protect at all, so anything that can reach this function with attacker-chosen text (this endpoint, or any future caller) is fully exploitable regardless of what the current frontend happens to send
Yes — since the only real caller sends a small, fixed set of values from a dropdown, there's no attacker-reachable path here
It's only unsafe if `sort_by` also needs to be quoted, which column names don't

feedback.identifier-injection-unfixable-by-bindin: Correct. Whether the current frontend restricts its own requests is a UI-layer convention, not a security boundary — anything that can send an HTTP request to this endpoint directly (a different client, a compromised frontend, a future caller nobody has reasoned about yet) can send any string. And critically, even reaching for parameterized binding wouldn't fix this: binding only ever protects a *value* position, never an identifier like a column name, so the fix here has to be a fixed allowlist of permitted values, checked in code before the string is ever built.
feedback.safe-because-dropdown: This confuses 'the current legitimate client happens to be well-behaved' with 'the endpoint is safe' — a server-side vulnerability doesn't depend on which client is calling it today. The dropdown is a UI convenience; it enforces nothing on the server, which is where the actual request is executed.
feedback.needs-quotes-to-escape: Column names in SQL generally don't need quoting, which is exactly the point being missed — the absence of a quoting requirement doesn't mean the position is safe, it means it's a completely different, and in some ways worse, category of injection risk, one that parameter binding is structurally unable to address.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Both `sort_by` and `direction` are identifier/keyword positions in the query, not value positions — an ORDER BY clause's column name and sort direction aren't things a database driver's parameter binding was ever built to substitute. That means the standard injection fix (bind the value) is unavailable here regardless of how the fix is applied; the only real defense is validating `sort_by` and `direction` against a small, explicit allowlist of the columns and directions the query actually supports, before any string is built at all.

contentSections.body: SQL injection is a channel problem, not a quote problem — check every place a value reaches the query string, including unquoted numeric positions and identifier positions parameter binding can never protect.

contentSections.title: The ORM doesn't save you by default

contentSections.body:
A specific, common false confidence: "this project uses an ORM, so it's not vulnerable to SQL injection." An ORM's normal query-builder methods (`.filter()`, `.where()`, `.find()`) are indeed parameterized under the hood and genuinely safe for the values you pass them — but every ORM also ships an escape hatch for queries the builder can't express cleanly, and generated code reaches for that escape hatch constantly the moment a query needs a join condition, a computed column, or a dynamic sort the builder's API doesn't cover neatly. The moment an f-string or string concatenation enters that raw-query method, every protection the ORM otherwise provides is gone for that one query — the ORM's safety is a property of specific methods, not a property of having chosen an ORM.

The review implication: seeing `.raw(`, `.execute(text(`, `session.execute(`, or any similarly named raw-SQL escape hatch in a diff is a specific, high-value signal to stop and check exactly how the string was built — the same way the earlier module treated a symmetric code structure as a specific signal to check every reference. An ORM project with a hundred safe `.filter()` calls and one raw query built with an f-string is exactly as exploitable through that one query as a project that never used an ORM at all.

contentSections.scenario: A generated Django view mixes ORM query-builder calls with a couple of raw queries for cases the builder didn't handle cleanly.
contentSections.question: Select every line where SQL injection is actually possible, assuming `request.GET` values are fully attacker-controlled.

items.label: `Order.objects.filter(customer_id=request.GET['customer_id'])`
`Order.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = {request.GET['customer_id']}")`
`Order.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s", [request.GET['customer_id']])`
`Order.objects.filter(status='active').extra(where=[f"region = '{request.GET['region']}'"])`

explanation.line-filter: The standard ORM query-builder method — `filter()` parameterizes its arguments under the hood, the same way a hand-written parameterized query does. Safe regardless of what `customer_id` contains.
explanation.line-raw-fstring: The raw-query escape hatch, fed an f-string. This is exactly as exploitable as a hand-written raw SQL string built the same way — the fact that it's called through `Order.objects` rather than a bare `db.execute` provides no protection at all.
explanation.line-raw-param: Also the raw-query escape hatch, but fed a parameterized query with the value passed separately as a bound argument (`[request.GET['customer_id']]`) rather than interpolated into the string — this is the safe way to use the raw-query method when the builder can't express what you need.
explanation.line-extra: `.extra()` is Django's older, explicitly-flagged-as-risky escape hatch for exactly this kind of raw SQL fragment, and an f-string inside it is just as exploitable as the `.raw()` case — the specific ORM method name matters less than whether a string was concatenated before the driver saw it.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of these four lines use the ORM's safe, parameterized query-builder surface and are fine regardless of input. Two use an escape hatch, and within those two, the one built with an f-string is exploitable and the one built with a separate parameter list is not — the ORM doesn't distinguish these for you, and neither does 'this project uses an ORM' as a blanket safety claim. The check has to be per query, not per project.

contentSections.body: "This project uses an ORM" is not a safety property — an ORM's raw-query escape hatch is exactly as vulnerable as hand-written SQL the moment a string gets built with concatenation or an f-string instead of a bound parameter.

title: Parameterisation, and why escaping is not the same fix
description: The actual mechanism that closes SQL injection completely, and why manually escaping dangerous characters is a different, weaker strategy that generated "safer" code sometimes reaches for instead.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why parameter binding closes injection entirely while character escaping only closes the specific characters it accounts for
Rewrite a concatenated query as a parameterized one across common query-builder and raw-driver interfaces

contentSections.body:
After a review flags string-built SQL, a generated "fix" arrives:

```python
def get_user(username):
    escaped = username.replace("'", "''")
    return db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{escaped}'")
```

This genuinely closes the exact exploit that was demonstrated — a single quote can no longer terminate the string early. It is still building SQL by gluing a request-controlled string into a command, and every other special character that context might care about (a backslash on some drivers, a byte sequence in an unusual encoding, a comment sequence) is still unhandled — the fix removed one working exploit and left the entire mechanism that produces exploits fully intact.

Escaping and parameter binding solve the same visible symptom through genuinely different mechanisms, and the difference matters even though both can make the exact same demonstrated attack fail. Escaping transforms specific dangerous characters within a string *before* it's concatenated into the command — it's a per-character patch, applied in application code, and it's correct only to the extent that every character the target context actually treats as special has been accounted for, correctly, for that specific database and that specific quoting context.
