steps.why: A record that exists but belongs to someone else and a record that doesn't exist at all should look identical to the caller — responding 404 either way avoids confirming that a given id exists for someone else's account.

faded.problem: Apply the same fix to the write version of this route: `router.patch('/api/invoices/:id', requireAuth, async (req, res) => { const invoice = await Invoice.findByIdAndUpdate(req.params.id, req.body, { new: true }); res.json(invoice); });`

blanks.prompt: What's the scoped equivalent of `findByIdAndUpdate` here — the call that only updates a document matching both the id and the requester?
blanks.answer: Invoice.findOneAndUpdate({ _id: req.params.id, userId: req.user.id }, req.body, { new: true })
accept: findOneAndUpdate({ _id: req.params.id, userId: req.user.id }, req.body, { new: true })
blanks.why: Same shape as the GET fix: the ownership condition moves into the query's filter, not into a separate check run after the fact — that way the update itself is atomic with the ownership check, rather than checking ownership on one read and then updating on a second, separate call.

blanks.prompt: What should the handler do if `invoice` comes back null after this call?
blanks.why: Identical reasoning to the read path — a null result means either the id doesn't exist or it belongs to someone else, and the response shouldn't distinguish the two.

faded.procedure: For any write operation on a record identified by an id in the URL, the ownership condition belongs inside the same database call that performs the write, filtering on both the record's id and the requester's identity together — never as a separate lookup-then-write pair, which reopens a gap between the check and the action.

contentSections.body: Check every verb on a resource route separately — GET, PATCH, DELETE each need their own ownership-scoped query — and in a multi-tenant system, check that the record's own org or tenant field is filtered on, not just that the acting user belongs to some org.

title: Tokens, expiry, and what a stolen one still buys
description: A generated token issuer that signs and returns — and never designed for the moment, which will eventually arrive, when that token is in the wrong hands.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a stateless token with no expiry stays valid after a password reset, and why revocation requires a deliberate design choice
Evaluate design choices — expiry, storage location, claim scope — by how much access they leave a stolen token with

contentSections.title: The token that outlives the password

contentSections.body:
A bare `jwt.sign(payload, secret)` is a complete, runnable answer to the literal instruction "create a token," which is most of why generated auth code stops there — expiry, refresh, and revocation are a second, un-asked design decision layered on top of token *creation*, not part of it. JWTs are validated statelessly and cryptographically, with no database lookup on each request, which is exactly what makes them fast and horizontally scalable — and exactly what removes any natural place to revoke one, since there's no row anywhere that "this token is no longer valid" could be written to and checked against.

The two real answers to that gap are a short expiry paired with a refresh-token rotation (so a stolen access token is only useful for a narrow window, and the longer-lived refresh token can be revoked server-side), or a server-side denylist checked on every request (which reintroduces exactly the database lookup the stateless design was meant to avoid, as a deliberate tradeoff). A generated `jwt.sign` with no `expiresIn` and nothing tracking issued tokens implements neither — which isn't a partial version of a token lifecycle, it's the complete absence of one.

contentSections.scenario: Same system as the hook. A user's account is compromised through a stolen token. The team's incident response is to force a password reset for the affected account. A week later, requests are still arriving from the attacker's IP using what turns out to be the original stolen token.
contentSections.question: Why does resetting the password not stop the stolen token from working?

options.label: JWT verification checks the token's cryptographic signature against the signing secret — it never looks up the user's current password or session state in a database at all
The password reset itself must have failed silently somewhere in the flow
The team should have rotated JWT_SECRET during the reset, and the process just missed that step this one time

feedback.no-db-check: Correct. A JWT's validity, by design, is a self-contained cryptographic fact — verify the signature, check the expiry claim if one exists, done. Nothing in that process consults the user's row in the database, so nothing about the user's row (a new password hash, an 'account locked' flag) can affect whether an already-issued token still verifies.
feedback.reset-didnt-work: The reset can complete correctly — password hash updated, user can log in with the new password — and this symptom would still occur, because the reset was never the mechanism that was supposed to invalidate the old token. Assuming the reset failed sends the investigation looking in the wrong place.
feedback.wrong-secret-rotated: Rotating the signing secret would work, but it's a global, blunt instrument — it invalidates every token for every user simultaneously, not just the compromised account's. It's evidence of exactly the gap this lesson names: without a per-user or per-token revocation mechanism, the only lever available is one that affects everyone.

contentSections.mechanism: Revocation isn't a feature that comes bundled with issuing a token — it's a separate mechanism that has to be designed in, because a signed, stateless token's whole value is that it can be verified without consulting anything else. Any event that's supposed to end a token's validity early — logout, password reset, a suspected compromise — needs its own explicit path: a short expiry that limits the damage window regardless, or a server-side record (a denylist, a token version number stored on the user and embedded in the token, a refresh-token store) that verification checks in addition to the signature. Without one of those, 'the user reset their password' and 'this specific token is still valid' are two facts that simply don't talk to each other.

contentSections.body: A signed token's validity is a fact about the signature and nothing else, unless the code deliberately makes it check something more — an expiry, a denylist, a version number tied to the user's row. Without one of those, no action a user or an admin takes after the token was issued can end its validity early.

contentSections.title: What a stolen token still buys

contentSections.body:
Assume a token will eventually be read by someone it wasn't issued to — through an XSS payload, a compromised dependency, a misconfigured log, a browser extension — and evaluate every design decision by how much that gets them, not by whether it happens.

Storage location changes what's reachable by injected script: a token in `localStorage` is readable by any JavaScript running on the page, including a script an XSS vulnerability injected, because `localStorage` has no access restriction beyond same-origin. A token in an `httpOnly` cookie is invisible to JavaScript entirely — an XSS payload can't read it no matter what it executes — though `httpOnly` cookies are sent automatically by the browser on matching requests, which is what makes CSRF a separate concern for that storage choice, mitigated with its own defenses (a CSRF token, `SameSite` cookie attributes) rather than by avoiding cookies altogether. Claim scope changes what the token is *for*: a login token that carries full account privileges buys an attacker everything the account can do; a token issued for one narrow purpose — read-only access to a single resource, for instance — buys them only that, even if it's stolen with equal ease. None of these choices stop a token from ever being stolen. Each one changes what stealing it is actually worth.

contentSections.scenario: A team is redesigning token handling after the incident from the first pod. Four proposed changes are on the table.
contentSections.question: Select every change that genuinely reduces what an attacker gains from a single stolen token, as opposed to making the token itself harder to forge or steal in the first place.

items.label: Short-lived access tokens (minutes, not days) paired with a revocable refresh token
Storing the token in an httpOnly, secure cookie instead of localStorage
Issuing tokens with only the specific claims/permissions a given client actually needs, instead of full account access by default
Using a longer, higher-entropy signing secret
Serving the app exclusively over HTTPS

explanation.short-expiry: Directly reduces the value of a stolen token by shrinking its usable window — a token stolen five minutes before it expires is worth almost nothing, regardless of how it was stolen.
explanation.httponly-cookie: Removes an entire theft vector (JavaScript-readable storage) rather than limiting what a successfully stolen token can do — but it's included here because it changes what a *given class* of attack (XSS reading localStorage) actually gets the attacker: nothing, for this specific channel.
explanation.narrow-scope: A token scoped to exactly what its holder needs limits the blast radius of a leak to that scope — a stolen read-only, single-resource token buys far less than a stolen full-account session, even though both were equally easy or hard to steal.
explanation.longer-secret: Signing-secret strength protects against an attacker *forging* a valid token from scratch — a real and separate concern — but it does nothing for a token that was already correctly issued and then stolen. A stolen, validly-signed token verifies exactly the same regardless of how long the secret is.
explanation.https-only: HTTPS protects a token in transit, between the client and the server, from a network eavesdropper — genuinely necessary, and unrelated to what happens after a token has already reached an attacker through some other channel, like an XSS payload reading it out of the page it's already loaded in.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of the five items here prevent a specific theft channel; the other three change what the theft is worth once it happens, which is the frame this lesson is asking for. A secure system needs both kinds of defense, but only 'what does a stolen token still buy' catches the gap in a design that prevented nothing about theft and also did nothing to limit the payoff if theft happens anyway — which is exactly the shape of the no-expiry, full-scope, localStorage-stored token this lesson opened with.

contentSections.body: Design every token as though it will eventually be read by someone it wasn't issued to, and ask what that reader would be able to do with it, and for how long, before you ship — expiry, storage, and scope are the three levers that answer to that question directly.

title: Find the missing authorisation check in seven handlers
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: spot the missing or misplaced check across the module's four risk areas — authn/authz confusion, uniform middleware, secrets, object-level access, and token design.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's authorization, secret-handling, object-level access, and token design checks at speed against unfamiliar handlers

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's territory, in no particular order of difficulty — done in one sitting or spread out, nothing here expires.
If a drill needed the hint before the pattern clicked, that's the one worth watching for in your own next review — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Permission-audit a generated multi-user feature
description: Generate a real multi-user feature from an AI tool, then audit every endpoint against what it should require versus what it actually checks — including the secrets it touches and the tokens it issues.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's authorization and secret-handling checks to genuinely AI-generated multi-user code, not curated examples
Produce a reusable permission-audit document grounded in real endpoints you personally reviewed

contentSections.body: Every example this module used already had its defect flagged for you. A real permission audit doesn't come pre-labeled — it comes as a set of routes, and each one either checks what it should or it doesn't. This lab closes that gap: generate a genuinely new multi-user feature from an AI tool, then audit it, endpoint by endpoint, the way you'd actually be asked to before it shipped.

contentSections.title: Permission-audit a generated multi-user feature
contentSections.brief: Pick a small multi-user feature you'd genuinely want built — a shared task list, a team document library, a comments system with moderation, a shared calendar with invitees — something with at least five distinct endpoints and at least two roles or ownership relationships (owner vs. member, member vs. admin, or similar). Generate real code for it from an AI tool of your choice, including auth middleware and any token issuance. Audit every endpoint it produced: what check does the code actually make, and what check should it make, given who's supposed to be allowed to do what.
contentSections.deliverable: An audit listing every endpoint the generated feature exposes, the check it actually makes today, and the check it should make — plus a short note on any secret handling or token-lifecycle issue you found (or a documented 'checked, none found').

stages.title: Generate and inventory
stages.instructions: Generate the feature. List every endpoint it exposes with its method, path, and a one-line description of what it does. For each, note whether the action is naturally public, owner-scoped, or role-gated — before looking closely at what the code actually checks.
stages.checkpoint: Every endpoint is listed with its intended authorization shape (public / owner-scoped / role-gated) written down before the detailed review starts.

stages.title: Classify what the code actually checks
stages.instructions: For each endpoint, read the actual implementation and note exactly what check runs before the action executes: nothing, authentication only, an ownership comparison, a role comparison, or some combination. Flag every place where the check you found doesn't match the shape you predicted in stage 1.
stages.checkpoint: Every endpoint has its actual check documented, and every mismatch between predicted and actual shape is flagged.

stages.title: Trace the exploit and check secrets and tokens
stages.instructions: For each flagged mismatch, write the concrete exploit: what a specific other user, with a specific role, could do by calling this endpoint. Separately, scan the generated code for hardcoded secrets, secrets logged or returned in error responses, secrets reachable from any client-bundled file, and any token issuance with no expiry or no revocation path.
stages.checkpoint: Every flagged endpoint has a concrete exploit description, and the secrets/token scan has a result — found or genuinely checked-and-clean — written down.

stages.title: Write the audit and self-check
stages.instructions: Compress your findings into the deliverable: every endpoint, its actual check, its needed check, plus the secrets/token note. Self-check against the rubric below before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: The audit covers every endpoint from stage 1, and every finding names the concrete exploit or the concrete constraint that makes it safe.

rubric.criterion: Every endpoint the generated feature exposes appears in the audit
rubric.meets: The list in the deliverable matches the endpoint inventory from stage 1 exactly — nothing generated was left out because it looked fine on a glance.

rubric.criterion: Each endpoint's actual check and needed check are both stated concretely
rubric.meets: An entry names the real code doing the checking (or its absence) and the specific comparison — owner id, role, org membership — that should be there instead of a generic 'needs better auth.'

rubric.criterion: Every mismatch includes a concrete exploit, not a general risk statement
rubric.meets: An entry says what a specific other account could actually do — read invoice 4470, delete comment 118 — the way the lesson examples did, rather than 'this could be a security issue.'

rubric.criterion: Secrets and token handling are checked explicitly, not assumed clean
rubric.meets: The audit states what was actually scanned for (hardcoded keys, client-bundle exposure, log/error leakage, token expiry and revocation) and what was found, including a documented clean result where nothing turned up.

rubric.criterion: The audit is usable as a real review artefact going forward
rubric.meets: Someone other than you could hand this feature's next PR to the audit and check whether new endpoints follow the same pattern, without needing this module's lessons open beside it.

contentSections.body: An audit built from endpoints you personally generated and personally traced an exploit through is worth more than a checklist copied from someone else's examples — it's calibrated to what your own prompts actually produce, and you already know exactly what each finding looks like in real code.

title: Checkpoint — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Injection and Untrusted Input (the module immediately before this one), two from The Bugs AI Writes Most, further back in this phase. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's authorization, secrets, and token patterns alongside earlier modules' defect and injection patterns, without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: `requireAuth` middleware confirms a request carries a valid session. What question does it leave completely unanswered?

options.label: Whether this specific identity is allowed to do this specific thing to this specific resource
Whether the request came over HTTPS
Whether the session token is well-formed JSON

questions.explanation: Authentication middleware establishes identity and stops there. Authorization — comparing that identity against a resource's owner, or against the roles a specific action requires — is a separate check that has to be written explicitly; nothing about a valid session implies it.

questions.from: This module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: A team fixes a hardcoded Stripe key by moving it to an environment variable in the next commit. Is the original exposure resolved?

options.label: No — the key is still readable in the git history of the earlier commit and has to be rotated
Yes, once the current source no longer contains the literal key
Yes, as long as .env is added to .gitignore going forward

questions.explanation: Git preserves every prior version of every file. Removing a secret from the latest commit does nothing to the earlier commit where it was written — only rotating the key at the provider closes the exposure.

questions.from: This module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: Why doesn't switching an invoice id from a sequential integer to a UUID fix an unscoped `Invoice.findById(id)` lookup?

options.label: The query still returns any invoice matching the id regardless of who's asking; a UUID that leaks through any other channel grants exactly the same access
UUIDs aren't actually random enough to prevent guessing
It does fix it, as long as the UUID is version 4

questions.explanation: Obscuring the id changes how hard it is to discover; it does nothing to what the query checks once someone has it. The fix is scoping the query itself to the requester, e.g. `findOne({ _id: id, userId: req.user.id })`.

questions.from: This module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: A JWT is issued with no `expiresIn`. A user's password is reset after a suspected compromise. Why does the old token keep working?

options.label: JWT verification checks the token's signature against the signing secret, never the user's current password hash or session state in a database
The password reset must have failed silently
JWTs always remain valid for 24 hours after issuance regardless of settings

questions.explanation: A stateless token's validity is a self-contained cryptographic fact. Nothing about resetting a password changes the signing secret or consults a revocation list, so an already-issued token with no expiry keeps verifying exactly as before, unless the design explicitly adds a check that it does.

questions.from: Previous module — Injection and Untrusted Input
questions.prompt: Why can't parameter binding protect a dynamically-selected column name in an `ORDER BY` clause?

options.label: Binding only substitutes values into a fixed command shape — it has no mechanism for substituting identifiers like column or table names, which are part of the shape itself
Because `ORDER BY` clauses don't support parameters in any SQL dialect
Binding works fine for column names too, as long as the driver supports it

questions.explanation: Identifiers aren't values, so the fix has to be an explicit allowlist checked before the query is built, not a bound parameter — the same distinction this module drew between a value inside a query and a table name interpolated into one.

questions.from: Previous module — Injection and Untrusted Input
questions.prompt: What specifically makes `shell=True` (or Node's `exec()`) dangerous compared to the list/`execFile` form?

options.label: It hands the full interpolated string to a shell for parsing, so shell metacharacters in any interpolated value are interpreted as command syntax rather than passed through as literal text
It's slower, which gives an attacker more time to intervene
It only matters if the command being run is a destructive one like `rm`

questions.explanation: The shell is what turns a semicolon or pipe inside an interpolated value into command-chaining syntax; the list form never invokes a shell at all, so the same content stays inert.

questions.from: Previous module — Injection and Untrusted Input
questions.prompt: A display name is escaped correctly for HTML body content, then reused inside an `<a href="/profile?user={name}">` link. Why might it still be exploitable?

options.label: HTML-body escaping and URL encoding are different, unrelated transformations — a value safe for one context isn't automatically safe for the other
It can't be exploitable — once a value is escaped once, it's safe everywhere it's used
Only inline `<script>` contexts are ever actually at risk from unescaped values

questions.explanation: Body, attribute, URL, and script positions each need their own specific encoding. Being escaped correctly for one context says nothing about the others.

questions.from: Previous module — Injection and Untrusted Input
questions.prompt: Why doesn't prompt injection have a fix structurally equivalent to SQL parameter binding?

options.label: A language model's context has no formally enforced boundary separating trusted instructions from untrusted data — everything is one stream of tokens, unlike SQL's fixed external grammar a driver can operate below
It does have an equivalent fix; most frameworks just haven't implemented it yet
Prompt injection only affects models without tool access

questions.explanation: No architectural wall exists between instruction and data in a model's context, which is why the available mitigations reduce impact (scoped tools, human approval) rather than closing the channel the way binding closes SQL injection.

questions.from: Two modules back — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated retry helper is `for attempt in range(max_retries):` with `max_retries = 3`. How many total attempts does this actually make?

options.label: 3 — range(3) yields exactly three values, so the loop body runs three times total, regardless of what the variable name implies
4 — the name 'max_retries' implies retries in addition to the first attempt
It depends on whether the first attempt is counted separately elsewhere in the code

questions.explanation: `range(3)` yields 0, 1, 2 — three iterations. The variable name suggests 'retries beyond an initial try,' a common convention the code doesn't actually implement; counting what the loop does, not what the name implies, is the only reliable check.

questions.from: Two modules back — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated checkout function has zero conditionals and operates on a list of cart items. What should that absence of branching make you check first?

options.label: What happens when the list is empty — the single most common non-happy-path state a function meets
Whether the function's variable names are descriptive enough
Whether the function is fast enough for a large cart

questions.explanation: Zero conditionals in an edge-case-heavy domain is the structural tell for happy-path-only code, and an empty collection is usually the single most common non-happy-path input a function actually meets in production.

title: Two requests at once: the read-then-write that loses data
description: A generated update that reads a value, changes it in memory, and writes it back — correct every time it runs alone, and silently wrong the moment two copies run at the same instant.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a read-then-write sequence in generated code as a race condition risk under concurrent requests
Trace a specific interleaving of two concurrent requests that produces a lost update

contentSections.body:
An AI tool builds a "decrement stock on purchase" function:

```python
def purchase(product_id, qty):
    product = db.get(product_id)
    if product.stock >= qty:
        product.stock -= qty
        db.save(product)
        return True
    return False
```

Run it once, alone, against a product with 5 in stock: it correctly reduces stock to 3 for a 2-unit purchase. Run it twice, at the same instant, against that same product, each buying the last unit of a 1-in-stock item, and both requests can read `stock = 1`, both see `1 >= 1`, both write `stock = 0` back — two units sold from a product that only had one, because both requests based their decision on the same stale snapshot of the row.

This is a specific, nameable shape, not a synonym for "bug that only shows up sometimes": a read, a decision or computation based on that read, and a write back — where nothing prevents a second read from happening on the same underlying data before the first write completes. Generated code produces this constantly because it's the natural way to describe the logic in isolation — "check the stock, then reduce it" reads as one sequential step when you're reasoning about a single request, and a single request is exactly the frame a prompt like "write a function that decrements stock on purchase" puts the model in. Nothing in that framing mentions a second, concurrent caller, so nothing in the generated code defends against one.

The general shape recurs everywhere a value is read, changed, and written back without the database itself enforcing that no other write can happen in between: an account balance debited by reading the current balance and subtracting, a seat-booking count incremented the same way, a rate limiter counting requests by reading-then-writing a counter. Every one of these is fine under a load test that runs requests one at a time, and every one of them loses updates the moment two callers hit the same row close enough together — which, for anything popular enough to matter, is not a rare event, it's Tuesday.

contentSections.code:
def purchase(product_id, qty):
    product = db.get(product_id)
    if product.stock >= qty:
        product.stock -= qty
        db.save(product)
        return True
    return False
contentSections.question: Two requests both call `purchase(product_id=42, qty=1)` at nearly the same instant, against a product with `stock=1`. What's the actual defect, precisely?

options.label: Both requests can read the same `stock=1` value before either one's write lands, so both pass the `>=` check and both decrement — the check and the write aren't atomic together
The comparison should be `product.stock > qty` instead of `>=`
The code needs a `threading.Lock()` imported at the top of the file

feedback.stale-read: Correct. `db.get`, the `if`, and `db.save` are three separate operations with no guarantee nothing else touches this row between them. If both requests execute `db.get` before either executes `db.save`, both are reasoning from a `stock=1` world that's already gone stale by the time either write happens.
feedback.wrong-operator: `>=` is the correct comparison for 'is there enough stock to fulfill this quantity' — a purchase of exactly the remaining stock should succeed. The operator isn't what allows the double-sell; the gap between reading and writing is.
feedback.missing-lock-import: A lock is a genuinely plausible tool for part of a fix, but 'import a lock' isn't specific enough to be correct or incorrect on its own — a lock only helps if it's held across the read, the check, and the write as one unit, and if every code path touching this row acquires the same lock. Naming the tool without naming how it needs to be used doesn't identify the actual defect.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The function is entirely correct as a description of what should happen to a single, uncontested purchase — and that's exactly what makes the bug easy to miss: reading it top to bottom, in isolation, it looks like a straightforward check-then-act. The defect only exists in the gap between the read and the write, which is invisible unless you specifically ask what could happen to this same row from a second caller during that gap.

contentSections.body: Any function that reads a value, decides something based on it, and writes a changed value back is a race condition risk unless something guarantees no other write can land on that same row in between — reading the code alone, correctly, once, tells you nothing about whether that guarantee exists.

contentSections.title: The database already has the fix

contentSections.body:
The fix is rarely an application-level lock — those only work if every single code path touching the row remembers to acquire the same one, in the same order, which is a maintenance burden that quietly breaks the first time someone adds a new code path and doesn't know the convention exists. The reliable fix moves the check and the write into a single operation the database itself performs atomically, so there's no gap between them for a second request to land in.

Most relational databases support exactly this as a single statement: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - %s WHERE id = %s AND stock >= %s`, checked by inspecting the number of rows affected (zero means the condition failed and nothing was decremented) rather than by a separate `SELECT` beforehand. The comparison and the write happen as one atomic operation from the database's point of view — there is no window between them for another request's write to land, because there was never a separate read step to grow stale in the first place. The same pattern generalizes: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - %s WHERE id = %s AND balance >= %s`, `UPDATE seats SET booked = booked + 1 WHERE event_id = %s AND booked < capacity` — the condition and the mutation, expressed together, in the WHERE clause and the SET clause of one statement.

contentSections.scenario: A teammate proposes fixing the purchase function by wrapping it in a transaction: `with db.transaction(): product = db.get(product_id); if product.stock >= qty: product.stock -= qty; db.save(product)`. Under the default (READ COMMITTED) isolation level most relational databases ship with, does this actually prevent the double-sell from the hook?
contentSections.question: Why might wrapping the read-check-write in a transaction not be enough on its own?

options.label: Under READ COMMITTED, a transaction's read doesn't block a second transaction's read of the same row — both can still read the same pre-write value before either commits, unless the read itself acquires a row lock or the isolation level is raised
Transactions never help with race conditions of any kind, so this proposal doesn't address the problem at all
This specific race condition only occurs in NoSQL databases; any relational database's default settings already prevent it

feedback.read-committed-allows-it: Correct. A transaction boundary guarantees atomicity and a consistent view of already-committed data — it doesn't, by itself, stop a second transaction from reading the same row before the first one writes, under the isolation level most databases default to. The read needs to explicitly lock the row (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in Postgres/MySQL) or the fix needs to be the single atomic UPDATE from earlier in this lesson, which sidesteps the whole question by never having a separate read step.
feedback.transactions-dont-help-at-all: Transactions absolutely help with race conditions — they're the standard tool for making a group of operations atomic and consistent. The issue here is narrower: under the *default* isolation level, a transaction boundary alone doesn't make a read-then-write immune to a concurrent read landing in the gap. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, a stricter isolation level, or the single atomic UPDATE all genuinely fix it.
feedback.only-helps-nosql: This exact race condition occurs in relational databases under their default isolation level just as readily as anywhere else — READ COMMITTED, the default for Postgres and MySQL's InnoDB in common configurations, explicitly allows two transactions to read the same row before either writes. This isn't a NoSQL-specific gap.

contentSections.mechanism: A transaction guarantees that its own operations either all happen or none do, and that it doesn't see another transaction's uncommitted changes — it does not, under common default isolation levels, guarantee that no other transaction can read the same row concurrently. Two transactions can both perform their `SELECT` before either performs its `UPDATE`, each one correctly reasoning from a row that's about to be invalidated by the other. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` closes this by taking a row lock at read time, forcing a second transaction's read of the same row to wait; the single atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE` closes it more simply, by never introducing a separate read step at all.

contentSections.body: A transaction boundary alone doesn't make a read-then-write safe under the isolation level most databases default to — either lock the row explicitly at read time, or collapse the check and the write into one atomic statement so there's no separate read to grow stale.

title: Idempotency, retries, and the payment charged twice
description: A retry that's meant to recover from a dropped response — and can just as easily repeat an action that already succeeded, because the client has no way to tell 'the request failed' from 'the response never arrived.'

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a client retry after a timeout cannot distinguish a genuinely failed request from a succeeded one whose response was lost
Identify which generated operations need an idempotency key and design one for a specific endpoint

contentSections.body:
The core problem isn't the retry — retrying a failed network call is correct behavior, not a bug. The problem is that a timeout is ambiguous by nature: from the client's side, "the server never received the request," "the server received it, processed it, and the response was lost on the way back," and "the server is still processing it right now" are indistinguishable. A retry is the right response to the first case and the wrong response to the second, and the client has no information that tells these apart.

Generated retry logic reaches for exactly this shape by default because "retry on timeout" is a complete, reasonable-sounding answer to "make this API call more reliable," and the ambiguity of what a timeout actually means is easy to not think about at all when writing the retry in isolation. The fix isn't avoiding retries — it's making the *server* able to recognize a retried request as the same request, so that retrying is always safe regardless of what actually happened the first time.

contentSections.scenario: The `charge_with_retry` function from the hook, called once by a client, where the underlying `payment_api.charge()` call times out on the first attempt because the response was delayed, not because the charge failed.
contentSections.question: What does the client actually know, at the moment it decides to retry, about whether the first charge succeeded?

options.label: Nothing — a timeout means no response was received in time, which is consistent with the charge having failed, succeeded, or still being in progress
It knows the charge failed, because a successful charge would have returned before the timeout
It knows the charge succeeded, because most timeouts happen on the response leg, after processing completes

feedback.nothing: Correct. A timeout is defined by the absence of a response within a window, and that absence is consistent with several different server-side outcomes. The client's retry decision is being made with zero information about which of those outcomes actually happened.
feedback.failed: This is the tempting assumption that makes the bug ship — a timeout *feels* like a failure because the client didn't get what it wanted, but the payment provider's own processing has no obligation to fail just because the response happened to be slow or the connection happened to drop after it succeeded.
feedback.succeeded: This overcorrects in the other direction with equally little basis — some timeouts genuinely do happen because the request never reached the server, or because the server is still working on it. Neither optimistic nor pessimistic assumption is justified by a timeout alone.

contentSections.concept: Idempotency is what turns this genuine uncertainty into a non-problem: an idempotency key — a unique identifier the client generates once per logical operation and sends with every attempt, including retries — lets the server recognize 'I've already processed this exact request' and return the original result instead of charging again, regardless of how many times the client retries or why the first response was lost.

contentSections.body: A timeout tells the client nothing about whether the operation it requested actually happened — treat every retryable, state-changing operation as needing a way for the server to recognize a repeat, not as needing the client to guess correctly about what happened the first time.

An idempotency key has to be generated once, by the client, at the start of the logical operation — not regenerated on each retry attempt, which would defeat the entire purpose by giving each retry a different identity. The server stores a record of which keys it has already processed and what result each one produced; when a request arrives with a key already on file, the server returns the stored result immediately without re-executing the operation, whether that request is attempt one or attempt four of the same logical purchase.

Not every operation needs this. A `GET` request is naturally idempotent already — running it twice reads the same data and changes nothing, so retrying it freely is always safe. The operations that need an explicit key are the ones that change state in a way that isn't naturally safe to repeat: charging a card, sending an email, incrementing a counter, creating a resource. "Naturally safe to repeat" is itself worth checking concretely rather than assumed — `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 100` run twice produces the same end state both times (safe to retry as-is); `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10` run twice adds twenty, not ten (needs a key); the retry-safety of an operation is a property of what it actually does to the state, not of whether it looks like a simple update.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in order for adding idempotency to the `charge_with_retry` function from this lesson.
steps: Generate a unique idempotency key once, at the start of the checkout flow, before any charge attempt begins
Pass the same key with every attempt, including every retry, so the server sees identical keys for the same logical purchase
On the server, check whether a result is already stored for this key before processing the charge
If a stored result exists, return it directly and skip charging again; if not, process the charge and store the result under this key
contentSections.explanation: The key has to exist before the first attempt, or the first attempt and its retries would each generate a different key and look like different purchases to the server — which is the exact bug idempotency keys exist to prevent. Passing the same key on every retry is what lets the server recognize a repeat at all. The server-side check has to happen before the charge runs, not after, or the charge executes every time regardless of whether it's a genuine retry. Storing the result under the key is what makes every subsequent retry of this same purchase — not just the second one — safe, no matter how many times the network causes the client to retry.

contentSections.body: Before adding a retry to any state-changing call, ask whether repeating that exact operation twice produces the same end state as running it once — if not, the retry needs an idempotency key generated before the first attempt, not a hope that the timeout meant failure.

title: Time zones, clock skew, and dates that are off by a day
description: A generated date calculation that's correct on the developer's machine, in the developer's timezone, and wrong for a user, a server, or a scheduled job anywhere else.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a date or time calculation in generated code that silently assumes a single timezone
Distinguish naive datetimes from timezone-aware ones and explain what breaks when the two are mixed

contentSections.body:
A generated "is this the user's birthday today" check:

```python
def is_birthday_today(user):
    today = datetime.now().date()
    return user.birth_date.month == today.month and user.birth_date.day == today.day
```

`datetime.now()` returns the current time in whatever timezone the *server* is running in — commonly UTC on a cloud host. A user in California, at 8pm on the 14th local time, is at 4am UTC on the 15th. For roughly a third of every day, this check compares the user's birthday against a date that isn't "today" anywhere the user actually is — the birthday email either fires a day early, a day late, or not at all, depending on which side of midnight UTC the user's local evening happens to land on.

`datetime.now()` (and its equivalents — `new Date()` in JavaScript reflects the runtime's local timezone unless explicitly converted, `LocalDateTime.now()` in Java is deliberately timezone-naive) answers "what time is it here, on this machine," not "what time is it for the user this code is about." On a developer's laptop, "here" is the developer's own timezone, and every manual test happens to compare against a date that matches the developer's own clock — which is exactly why this class of bug passes local testing every time and only surfaces once real users in other timezones, a server in a different region, or a scheduled job running at a boundary hour are involved.

The deeper issue is the difference between a *naive* datetime (a `year/month/day/hour` with no attached timezone — is `2024-03-15 23:00` in Tokyo or in Toronto? the value alone can't say) and an *aware* one (a datetime carrying an explicit UTC offset or timezone identifier, unambiguous regardless of where it's read). Generated code defaults to naive datetimes because they're simpler to construct and the functions that produce them (`datetime.now()`, `date.today()`) are the shortest answer to "get the current time" — and naive datetimes are exactly the values that silently mean something different depending on where the code executing them happens to run.

contentSections.scenario: The `is_birthday_today` function passes every test the developer wrote, including tests specifically checking the 'today is the birthday' case, run at various times of day during development in the developer's own timezone.
contentSections.question: Why does this function pass every local test while still being wrong for users in other timezones?

options.label: Every test implicitly compares against `datetime.now()` in the same timezone the developer (and the eventual server) runs in — the tests never varied the assumption that 'today' means the same calendar date for the code and for the user
The tests simply don't cover enough different birthdate values
This only breaks once a year on each affected user's birthday, so it's a low-priority edge case not worth catching

feedback.same-timezone-assumed: Correct. A test run in the developer's own timezone, comparing against `datetime.now()` resolved in that same timezone, can never expose a bug that only appears when the *user's* timezone differs from the *server's* — the test and the code share the identical implicit assumption, so they always agree with each other regardless of whether that shared assumption is actually correct for a real user.
feedback.tests-poorly-written: More birthdate values wouldn't help — the bug isn't in which birthdates are tested, it's in which timezone 'today' is computed relative to. A hundred different birthdates tested from the same timezone would still all pass and still miss the actual defect.
feedback.rare-edge-case: The failure window isn't once a year — it's every single day, for the roughly one-third of a 24-hour period where the user's local date and the server's UTC date disagree, for every user outside the server's timezone. Whether a *specific* user's birthday falls during that window on a *specific* day is what's occasional; the underlying timezone mismatch is constant.

contentSections.mechanism: A test's blind spot generally isn't random — it's structurally identical to the blind spot in the code it's testing, because both were often written with the same implicit assumption in mind. Here, both the function and the test resolve 'today' the same way, in the same timezone, so no local test run can ever produce a disagreement between them. Catching this requires either testing with an explicitly different timezone context than the one the test happens to run in, or — better — designing the function to take the user's timezone as an explicit input rather than reaching for the ambient 'now' at all: `is_birthday_today(user, now=datetime.now(user.timezone))`.

contentSections.body: A date or time calculation that reaches for the ambient 'now' — `datetime.now()`, `new Date()` — is answering 'what time is it on this machine,' not 'what time is it for the person this code concerns.' Anywhere a date matters to a specific user, pass their timezone in explicitly rather than assuming the server's.

contentSections.title: Clock skew and the gap that isn't a timezone at all

contentSections.body:
A separate, related failure doesn't involve timezones at all: two machines' clocks simply disagreeing about what time it currently is, even when both are configured for the same timezone. A generated token-expiry check comparing a token's `issuedAt` timestamp (set by one server) against `datetime.now()` (read on a different server, or the same server after an unsynced clock drift) can reject a token as "not yet valid" or accept one as "not yet expired" based on a few seconds or minutes of clock disagreement that has nothing to do with the actual passage of time. This is common enough in distributed systems that it has a name — clock skew — and NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronization keeps it small in practice, but "small" is not "zero," and code that assumes two machines' clocks agree exactly is making a claim about infrastructure it has no actual guarantee of.

The practical defense for both timezone bugs and clock-skew bugs is the same instinct: store and compare timestamps in UTC everywhere internally, convert to a user's local timezone only at the point of display, and build a small tolerance window into any comparison where two different machines' clocks are involved (accept a token issued up to a minute "in the future" relative to this server's clock, rather than rejecting it outright) rather than treating clock agreement as exact.

contentSections.scenario: A generated JWT verification check rejects a token if `token.issuedAt > datetime.now()` — the token claims to have been issued in the future relative to this server's clock. Two servers in the same data center, synchronized via NTP under normal, healthy operating conditions, typically disagree on the current time by roughly how much?
contentSections.question: Predict the typical clock disagreement, in milliseconds, between two well-synchronized servers under normal conditions.
contentSections.explanation: Under healthy NTP synchronization, clock skew between two servers is typically well under 100 milliseconds — often in the tens of milliseconds. That's small, and also not zero: a token verification check with a hard `>` comparison and no tolerance window will occasionally, unpredictably reject a token issued a few milliseconds ago on a different server, purely because that server's clock is trivially ahead of this one's at the moment of comparison. A tolerance window of a few seconds (`token.issuedAt > datetime.now() + timedelta(seconds=5)`) absorbs normal clock skew without meaningfully weakening the check's actual security purpose, which is catching tokens genuinely issued far in the future, not ones issued a heartbeat ago on a slightly-ahead clock.

contentSections.body: Store and compare timestamps in UTC internally, convert to a user's local timezone only for display, and build a small tolerance into any comparison spanning two different machines' clocks — treating clock agreement as exact is a claim about infrastructure the code has no actual guarantee of.

title: Async code that awaits nothing, and errors that vanish
description: A generated function that calls an async operation, doesn't await it, and moves on — the call still happens, on its own schedule, with no connection left to anything that could catch what it does wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a missing await on a promise/coroutine and explain the specific consequence for both ordering and error handling
Recognize an unhandled promise rejection as a swallowed error, distinct from an exception that was actually caught and handled

contentSections.body:
A missing `await` is not the same failure as a missing `try`/`catch` — it's earlier and quieter than that. A `try`/`catch` around code that runs synchronously (or that's properly awaited) will catch whatever that code throws, at the moment it throws it, in the calling function's own control flow. An unawaited promise's rejection happens on its own schedule, disconnected from the caller's control flow entirely — by the time it rejects, the function that called it may have already returned, and there is no `catch` block anywhere in the codebase positioned to receive it, because a `catch` can only receive what an `await` (or an explicit `.catch()`) hands to it.

Generated code drops the `await` most often on a call whose result isn't used — exactly the case here, where nothing reads the return value of `sendConfirmation`, so nothing in the surrounding code's data flow visibly depends on it finishing. A function call whose result is used almost always gets awaited, because leaving it unawaited would make the very next line fail obviously (using a promise object where a value was expected) — it's specifically the fire-and-forget calls, valuable exactly because their side effect matters, where the missing await is easiest to write and hardest to notice on a read-through.

contentSections.question: What's the concrete, specific consequence of the missing `await` on this line, beyond "it's not awaited"?

options.label: If `sendConfirmation` rejects, nothing in this function (or anywhere) is positioned to catch it — the rejection happens after `createOrder` may have already returned, disconnected from any surrounding try/catch
The order itself won't actually be created, since the function returns before the email finishes sending
This is a style issue only — `sendConfirmation` will still run to completion exactly as if it were awaited

feedback.unreachable-rejection: Correct. `order` is already created and awaited correctly on the line above — that part isn't affected. The actual consequence is specifically about error handling and ordering for the email send: a rejection from `sendConfirmation` has no `await` or `.catch()` positioned to receive it, so it's effectively invisible to this function and to any error handling wrapped around calling it.
feedback.order-not-created: The order creation (`await db.orders.create(orderData)`) is awaited correctly on the previous line and completes before this line even runs — that part of the function is fine. The missing await is specifically on the email call, one line later.
feedback.purely-stylistic: The call does still execute — that part is correct — but 'runs exactly as if awaited' isn't true for two things that matter: the function no longer waits for it to finish before returning (an ordering difference), and any rejection it produces has no connected `catch` (an error-handling difference). Both are real behavioral differences, not style.

contentSections.flawExplanation: `emailService.sendConfirmation(...)` without `await` still gets called — the function invocation happens immediately, synchronously, as part of running this line. What's missing is the *connection* between that call's eventual outcome (success or rejection) and anything in this function's control flow. The promise it returns is simply discarded, which is fine if it resolves and invisible if it rejects.

contentSections.body: Check every async call whose return value isn't used for an `await` in front of it — those are exactly the calls where a missing await is easiest to write and hardest to notice, and exactly the calls where its rejection has the fewest places left to be caught.

Adding `await` everywhere isn't automatically the right fix, either — it changes the function's ordering guarantees, which matters when the caller genuinely shouldn't wait on a side effect that isn't essential to the response. If `createOrder` should return to the customer immediately, without making them wait on an email provider's round trip, blindly awaiting `sendConfirmation` inline is a real regression: a slow or down email provider now makes order creation itself slow or appear to fail, for a step that was never supposed to be on the critical path.

The actual fix depends on which of those two shapes the operation needs, and it's worth naming explicitly rather than defaulting to either: if the caller needs to know the email succeeded before returning, `await` it and handle the rejection where it's awaited. If the caller genuinely shouldn't wait, the call still needs its rejection handled *somewhere* — attach an explicit `.catch()` right there (`emailService.sendConfirmation(order.email, order.id).catch(err => logger.error('confirmation email failed', { orderId: order.id, err }))`), so the error is captured and observable instead of vanishing, even though the function itself doesn't wait for the outcome.

contentSections.scenario: Four ways of calling the same fire-and-forget-eligible `sendConfirmation(order.email, order.id)` line inside `createOrder`, which should return to its own caller without waiting on the email.
contentSections.question: Select every version that correctly returns without waiting on the email, while still capturing a rejection instead of losing it.

items.label: `emailService.sendConfirmation(order.email, order.id);` with nothing else
`await emailService.sendConfirmation(order.email, order.id);`
`emailService.sendConfirmation(order.email, order.id).catch(err => logger.error('confirmation email failed', { orderId: order.id, err }));`
Wrapping the bare, unawaited call in a synchronous `try { ... } catch (err) { ... }` block around it

explanation.bare-call: This is the original bug — returns without waiting, correctly, but any rejection is completely unconnected to anything and is lost.
explanation.await-inline: This does capture the outcome, but it also makes `createOrder` wait for the email to finish before returning — which is the opposite of 'fire-and-forget,' and reintroduces the exact latency coupling this design was trying to avoid.
explanation.catch-attached: This is the correct shape: the function doesn't wait for `sendConfirmation` to resolve before returning `order`, and the `.catch()` is still attached to the promise, so a rejection is captured and logged whenever it eventually happens, rather than vanishing.
explanation.try-catch-wrap: A synchronous `try/catch` only catches errors thrown *synchronously*, during the initial, immediate part of calling `sendConfirmation` — it has no ability to catch a rejection that happens later, asynchronously, after this line has already finished executing and control has moved on. This looks like error handling and structurally cannot function as any.

contentSections.synthesis: Exactly one of these four keeps the function's ordering unaffected (returns immediately, doesn't block on the email) while still giving the rejection somewhere to go. The other three either reintroduce the original bug in a new shape, accidentally add a blocking wait nobody asked for, or add code that looks like error handling but is structurally incapable of catching what it's aimed at.

contentSections.body: Decide explicitly whether a caller needs to wait on an async side effect before deciding how to handle its errors — `await` it if the caller needs the outcome, attach an explicit `.catch()` if it doesn't, but never leave a promise both unawaited and uncaught.

title: Transactions: what is actually atomic here
description: A generated multi-step operation wrapped in what looks like a transaction — where one of the steps was never actually inside it, or the whole thing was never atomic with an external call it depends on.

learningObjectives.text: Trace exactly which operations are and aren't covered by a given transaction boundary in generated code
Identify the specific partial-failure state a transaction cannot protect against when it wraps a database write alongside a call to an external, non-transactional system

contentSections.body:
A generated "transfer funds between accounts" function:

```python
def transfer(from_id, to_id, amount):
    with db.transaction():
        from_account = db.get(from_id)
        from_account.balance -= amount
        db.save(from_account)
    to_account = db.get(to_id)
    to_account.balance += amount
    db.save(to_account)
```

It reads like a transaction wraps the transfer. It wraps exactly one of the two account updates — the `with db.transaction():` block closes after `db.save(from_account)`, and the credit to `to_account` happens entirely outside it, as two separate, unprotected database calls. If the process crashes, or the credit call fails, between those two blocks, the money has left one account and never arrived at the other — visibly, permanently, with no transaction boundary left to roll either side back.

The word "transaction" appearing in generated code is not the same claim as "this multi-step operation is atomic." A transaction only covers the operations that are lexically inside its boundary, and generated code frequently produces a transaction block that looks like it covers a whole operation while actually covering only its first part — the indentation and the `with`/`try` structure reads as encompassing everything nearby, even when the code after the block's closing line is doing work that logically belongs to the same operation.

The review check is mechanical and specific: for any code claiming transactional behavior, trace exactly which statements are lexically inside the transaction's scope — inside the `with` block, inside the `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` pair, inside the function passed to whatever transaction-running helper is in use — and which are outside it, regardless of how close together they appear or how clearly they read as one logical step. Anything outside the boundary gets none of the transaction's guarantees, no matter how naturally it belongs there.

contentSections.code:
def transfer(from_id, to_id, amount):
    with db.transaction():
        from_account = db.get(from_id)
        from_account.balance -= amount
        db.save(from_account)
    to_account = db.get(to_id)
    to_account.balance += amount
    db.save(to_account)
contentSections.question: What's the precise scope problem here?

options.label: The `with db.transaction():` block closes after the debit is saved — the credit to `to_account` runs entirely outside the transaction, as unprotected, independent database calls
The debit and credit are performed in the wrong logical order — credit should happen before debit
The function doesn't validate that `amount` is positive before transferring

feedback.scope-ends-early: Correct. Everything after the `with` block's indentation ends is outside the transaction, full stop — `to_account`'s read and write are two separate, ordinary database calls with no atomicity relationship to the debit above them, or to each other.
feedback.wrong-order: Reordering wouldn't fix anything — it would just move which half of the transfer is protected and which half isn't. The actual defect is that only one half is ever inside the transaction boundary, regardless of which one it is.
feedback.missing-validation: A real gap worth adding — a negative `amount` would credit the 'to' account by subtracting from the 'from' account backward — but it's a separate concern from the atomicity problem, which would exist identically even with perfect input validation in place.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A transaction is defined by its lexical boundary, not by what a reader infers the code is 'trying' to do as one unit. `db.save(from_account)` is the last statement inside the `with` block; every line after it, however closely related in intent, executes with no relationship to that transaction at all.

contentSections.body: Before trusting that a multi-step operation is atomic, trace exactly which statements sit inside the transaction's actual lexical boundary — a variable name, a comment, or physical proximity to the `with`/`BEGIN` block tells you nothing about whether a given line is actually covered by it.

contentSections.title: The boundary a database transaction can't reach

contentSections.body:
Fixing the scope so both account updates sit inside one transaction solves the version of this bug that's purely a database problem — but the same shape recurs, unfixable the same way, whenever one of the two "halves" of an operation isn't a database write at all. A generated checkout function that saves an order to the database and then calls an external payment provider's API, or a signup function that creates a user record and then calls a third-party email service to send a welcome message, has exactly the same partial-failure shape as the transfer function — and no database transaction, however correctly scoped, can roll back a request that's already been sent to and processed by a system outside the database entirely. `db.transaction()` can undo a `db.save()`; it has no mechanism whatsoever for undoing an HTTP request a payment provider already received and acted on.

This is a fundamentally different kind of atomicity problem, and it doesn't have a version of the earlier fix — there's no boundary you can widen to cover it, because the two systems involved (your database, their API) don't share one. The two real answers are ordering the operations so the *external, harder-to-undo* action happens last, after the database state it depends on is already durably committed (so a failure after the external call at least leaves a consistent, resumable local state), and treating the whole operation as a saga — a sequence of steps with an explicit compensating action for each one (a refund call, a cancellation email) that runs if a later step fails, rather than assuming any single boundary makes the whole thing atomic.

contentSections.scenario: A generated checkout function: `order = db.orders.create(cart, status='pending'); payment = payment_provider.charge(cart.total, card_token); db.orders.update(order.id, status='paid');` — no explicit transaction anywhere. Assume the payment provider is a third-party HTTP API with no relationship to this database.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that's actually true about this function's atomicity, given that a database transaction can't span the external payment call.

items.label: Wrapping all three lines in `with db.transaction():` would make the payment call atomic with the database writes
Creating the order as 'pending' before charging means a crash after the charge at least leaves a resumable local record, rather than a charge with no order to reconcile it against

If the process crashes after `payment_provider.charge()` succeeds but before the final `db.orders.update()` runs, the customer is charged and the order is stuck at 'pending' — a state that needs an explicit reconciliation step to detect and resolve, not a rollback
If this operation is ever retried after a partial failure, the charge call itself needs an idempotency key so a retry doesn't charge the customer a second time

explanation.no-tx-helps-payment: A database transaction can only roll back operations the database itself performed. `payment_provider.charge()` is an HTTP call to a system with its own, entirely separate state — no `db.transaction()` boundary, however widely drawn, has any mechanism for undoing a charge that's already been processed on the provider's side.
explanation.order-first-safe-ish: This ordering choice doesn't make the operation atomic, but it does make a partial failure *diagnosable and resumable*: a 'pending' order with no matching successful charge is a state a reconciliation job can find and act on, which is the practical, honest substitute for atomicity when true atomicity isn't available.
explanation.charge-then-crash: This is exactly the partial-failure state this design has to be built to survive, not prevented from occurring — because it structurally can't be prevented across two independent systems. The order is stuck 'pending' with an actual successful charge behind it, and something (a webhook from the payment provider, a periodic reconciliation sweep) needs to notice and update it.
explanation.idempotent-charge-needed: Directly connects to the earlier lesson on retries in this module — any retry of this operation after a partial failure needs the charge call itself to be safe to repeat, or a retry after the payment succeeded but the local update failed would charge the customer twice while trying to fix a bookkeeping problem.

contentSections.synthesis: None of the four true-or-false claims here are about finding a bigger transaction boundary — because there isn't one available. Once an operation spans a system outside the database, the honest design goal shifts from 'atomic' to 'ordered so failure is diagnosable, and safe to retry without duplicating the irreversible part' — which is a real, different, achievable property, just not the one 'wrap it in a transaction' promises.

contentSections.body: A database transaction can only ever cover operations the database itself performs. Once a multi-step operation includes a call to an external system, order the harder-to-undo action last against durably committed local state, and design for detecting and resolving the partial-failure state explicitly — there's no boundary left to make the whole thing atomic.
