title: Make a generated booking flow safe under simultaneous use
description: Take a generated booking or reservation flow, find the interleaving of two simultaneous requests that breaks it, and fix it so the guarantee holds under real concurrent load, not just in a single-request test.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a specific interleaving of two concurrent requests that produces an incorrect outcome in generated booking code
Produce a corrected version of the flow that holds its guarantee under the interleaving that broke the original

contentSections.body: Every race condition this module used was already found and written up for you, with the interleaving spelled out in advance. Finding one yourself means holding two requests in your head at once and working out, step by step, whether they can land in an order that breaks the guarantee the code is supposed to provide. This lab is that exercise against real generated code: a booking flow you generate yourself, and the specific interleaving that breaks it.

contentSections.title: Make a generated booking flow safe under simultaneous use
contentSections.brief: Generate a small booking or reservation flow from an AI tool — appointment slots, event seats, a shared meeting room, limited-quantity tickets — anything with a finite capacity that two people could plausibly try to claim at the same time. Get the generated version working for a single request first. Then find the specific interleaving of two simultaneous requests that lets the capacity be oversold or double-booked, fix the flow so it holds under that interleaving, and write up both.
contentSections.deliverable: A corrected version of the flow, plus a written description of the exact interleaving (which request reads what, when, relative to the other) that broke the original.

stages.title: Generate and verify the single-request case
stages.instructions: Generate the booking flow. Confirm it works correctly for one request at a time: booking succeeds when capacity remains, and correctly fails once capacity is exhausted.
stages.checkpoint: The flow is confirmed correct under sequential, one-at-a-time use before any concurrency is introduced.

stages.title: Find the interleaving that breaks it
stages.instructions: Read the flow for a read-then-write, check-then-act shape — is availability checked and then decremented as separate steps? Write out, explicitly, an interleaving of two simultaneous requests (which line each executes, in what order relative to the other) that results in overbooking. If you have the tooling to actually run two concurrent requests and reproduce it, do that; if not, the traced interleaving on paper is the required artefact.
stages.checkpoint: A specific, step-by-step interleaving is written down that would result in overbooking, naming which request does what at each point.

stages.title: Fix it
stages.instructions: Rewrite the flow so the interleaving from stage 2 can no longer produce an incorrect outcome — an atomic conditional update, a row lock, or an equivalent mechanism for your stack. Confirm the single-request case from stage 1 still works correctly after the fix.
stages.checkpoint: The corrected flow closes the specific interleaving found in stage 2, and the original single-request behavior still works.

stages.title: Write it up and self-check
stages.instructions: Write the deliverable: the corrected code and the interleaving description. Self-check against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: The write-up names the exact broken interleaving and shows the specific mechanism that now prevents it.

rubric.criterion: The flow is generated, real code — not a hypothetical or a curated example
rubric.meets: The deliverable includes the actual generated code you started from, not a paraphrase or a remembered example from the lessons.

rubric.criterion: The broken interleaving is specific and step-by-step
rubric.meets: The write-up names which request executes which line at each point, the way this module's own examples did — not a general statement like 'there could be a race condition here.'

rubric.criterion: The fix targets the actual interleaving found, not a generic hardening pass
rubric.meets: The corrected version specifically closes the gap the interleaving exploited — an atomic conditional update or explicit lock at the exact point the original had a read-then-write gap.

rubric.criterion: The single-request case still works after the fix
rubric.meets: The corrected flow was re-verified against ordinary, one-at-a-time use, not just against the concurrent case, confirming the fix didn't just move the bug.

rubric.criterion: The write-up is usable by someone else reviewing similar generated code
rubric.meets: Someone other than you could read the interleaving description and understand exactly what made the original code unsafe, without this module's lessons open beside it.

contentSections.body: A booking flow that works correctly for one request at a time and a booking flow that's actually safe are different claims, and the gap between them is only visible once you deliberately hold two requests in your head and trace what each one sees of the other.

title: Checkpoint — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Auth, Secrets and Permissions, two from further back in this phase. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's race-condition, idempotency, timezone, async, and transaction-scope patterns alongside earlier modules' authorization and defect patterns, without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: Two requests both call a `purchase()` function that reads stock, checks it, then writes a decremented value back, against a product with 1 unit left. Under the default relational isolation level, why can both requests succeed?

options.label: Both requests can read the same pre-write stock value before either one's write lands, so both pass the availability check based on the same now-stale snapshot
The `>=` comparison operator is incorrect and should be `>`
This can only happen if the database has no transaction support at all

questions.explanation: The read, the check, and the write are three separate operations with no guarantee nothing else touches the row between them — the fix is an atomic conditional UPDATE or an explicit row lock at read time, not a different comparison operator.

questions.from: This module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: A payment request times out because the response was delayed, not because the charge failed, and the client retries. What does the client actually know about whether the first charge succeeded at the moment it decides to retry?

options.label: Nothing — a timeout is consistent with the charge having failed, succeeded, or still being processed
It knows the charge failed, since a successful charge would have returned before timing out
It knows the charge succeeded, since most timeouts happen after processing completes

questions.explanation: A timeout is defined purely by the absence of a response in time, which is consistent with several different server-side outcomes — the fix is an idempotency key generated before the first attempt, so a retry is always safe regardless of what actually happened.

questions.from: This module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: A generated 'is this the user's birthday today' check uses `datetime.now()` on the server. Why does this pass every test the developer runs locally, while still being wrong for users in other timezones?

options.label: The test and the code share the same implicit assumption — both resolve 'today' in the developer's own timezone, so they always agree with each other regardless of whether that's correct for a real user elsewhere
The tests don't cover enough different birthdate values
This bug is rare enough that testing wouldn't reasonably be expected to catch it

questions.explanation: A test's blind spot is often structurally identical to the blind spot in the code, because both share the same implicit assumption — comparing against the ambient 'now' in whichever timezone the code happens to run in, rather than the user's actual timezone passed in explicitly.

questions.from: This module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: A generated `transfer(from_id, to_id, amount)` function wraps only the debit to `from_account` inside `with db.transaction():`, with the credit to `to_account` running as separate calls after the block closes. What's the precise defect?

options.label: Everything after the transaction block's closing line is outside it and gets none of its guarantees, regardless of how naturally it reads as part of the same operation
The debit and credit are performed in the wrong logical order
The function is missing input validation on `amount`

questions.explanation: A transaction only covers what's lexically inside its boundary — proximity or apparent intent doesn't extend it. Both account updates need to sit inside the same transaction block for the transfer to actually be atomic.

questions.from: Previous module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: `requireAuth` middleware confirms a request carries a valid session. What question does it leave completely unanswered?

options.label: Whether this specific identity is allowed to do this specific thing to this specific resource
Whether the request came over HTTPS
Whether the session token is well-formed

questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity and stops there — authorization, comparing that identity against a resource's owner or the roles a specific action requires, is a separate check that has to be written explicitly.

questions.from: Previous module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: A team fixes a hardcoded API key by moving it to an environment variable in the next commit. Is the original exposure resolved?

options.label: No — the key is still readable in the git history of the earlier commit and has to be rotated
Yes, once the current source no longer contains the literal key
Yes, as long as .env is added to .gitignore going forward

questions.explanation: Git preserves every prior version of every file — removing a secret from the latest commit does nothing to the earlier commit where it was written. Only rotating the key at the provider closes the exposure.

questions.from: Previous module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: Why doesn't switching a record's id from a sequential integer to a UUID fix an unscoped `findById(id)` lookup?

options.label: The query still returns any matching record regardless of who's asking; a UUID that leaks through any other channel grants exactly the same access
UUIDs aren't random enough to actually prevent guessing
It does fix it, as long as the UUID is version 4

questions.explanation: Obscuring the id changes how hard it is to discover; it does nothing to what the query checks once someone has it. The fix scopes the query itself to the requester.

questions.from: Previous module — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: A JWT is issued with no `expiresIn`. A user's password is reset after a suspected compromise. Why does the old token keep working?

options.label: JWT verification checks the token's signature against the signing secret, never the user's current password hash or session state in a database
The password reset must have failed silently
JWTs always remain valid for 24 hours after issuance regardless of settings

questions.explanation: A stateless token's validity is a self-contained cryptographic fact — nothing about resetting a password changes the signing secret or consults a revocation list unless the design explicitly adds one.

questions.from: Three modules back — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated 'last N days' filter subtracts N full days and then uses `>=` to include the boundary date. What's the general shape of this defect?

options.label: Mixing an inclusive requirement with an exclusive-style offset — the result spans N+1 dates instead of N
Using `>=` instead of `>`, which is always wrong for date filtering
A timezone bug, since it doesn't specify a timezone

questions.explanation: The offset and the inclusive comparison don't agree with each other — the fix adjusts the offset by one, not the operator, which was already correct for the inclusive requirement.

questions.from: Two modules back — Injection and Untrusted Input
questions.prompt: What specifically makes `shell=True` (or Node's `exec()`) dangerous compared to the list/`execFile` form?

options.label: It hands the full interpolated string to a shell for parsing, so shell metacharacters in any interpolated value are interpreted as command syntax rather than passed through as literal text
It's slower, which gives an attacker more time to intervene
It only matters if the command being run is a destructive one like `rm`

questions.explanation: The shell is what turns a semicolon or pipe inside an interpolated value into command-chaining syntax; the list form never invokes a shell at all, so the same content stays inert.

title: The catch block that swallows the error and returns null
description: A generated try/catch that turns a real, specific failure into an empty return value — quiet at the point of failure, and expensive several layers up, where nobody knows a failure ever happened.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a catch block that discards an exception's information and returns a value indistinguishable from a legitimate empty result
Explain why a caller receiving null cannot distinguish 'nothing found' from 'the lookup itself failed'

contentSections.body:
A bare `except Exception: return None` (or its equivalents — a blanket `catch (err) { return null; }`, a `rescue => nil`) is a complete, runnable answer to "handle the error so the program doesn't crash," which is most of why it's the reflexive shape generated code reaches for: it satisfies the literal instruction to not let an exception propagate, at the lowest possible cost in code. What it doesn't do is preserve any information about *what* failed, and collapsing every possible failure — a network blip, a malformed query, a permissions error, a genuinely empty result — into the identical return value is not error handling, it's error deletion.

The review question worth asking isn't "does this have a try/catch" — nearly all generated code that touches I/O does. It's "can the caller, or a human reading a log five minutes after an incident, tell the difference between 'this legitimately found nothing' and 'this failed and I have no idea why'?" If the answer is no, the catch block has made the system harder to debug than having no error handling at all, because the absence of a crash reads as evidence that everything worked.

contentSections.question: A caller does `prefs = get_user_preferences(user_id); if prefs is None: apply_defaults()`. What's the actual defect in this design?

options.label: `None` is returned both when the query genuinely finds no rows and when the query itself failed — the caller cannot tell these two situations apart, and silently applies defaults in both cases
The database query should be made asynchronous so it doesn't block the request thread during an outage
The f-string interpolation of user_id is a SQL injection risk, which is the main problem here

feedback.same-value-two-meanings: Correct. 'No preferences exist for this user' and 'the database couldn't be reached' are two entirely different facts about the world, and this function reports them identically. A caller applying default preferences because of an outage, believing it's applying them for a legitimate reason, is masking an incident as normal behavior.
feedback.should-use-async: Async versus sync execution is a real performance and architecture question, and orthogonal to this lesson's actual defect — a fully async version of this same function, with the identical bare except-return-None pattern, has exactly the same information-loss problem.
feedback.fstring-injection: A genuine, separate defect — interpolating `user_id` directly into the query string is exactly the SQL injection pattern from an earlier module in this phase — but it's not what this lesson is about, and fixing it wouldn't touch the error-swallowing problem, which would exist identically in a fully parameterized version of this query.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The bug isn't the presence of a catch block — catching the exception so a database outage doesn't crash the whole request is reasonable. The bug is what happens inside it: every possible cause of failure is compressed into a single, silent, semantically-overloaded `None`, indistinguishable from a legitimate empty result, with the actual exception — its type, its message, the fact that it happened at all — discarded before anyone or anything downstream ever sees it.

contentSections.body: Before trusting a catch block, ask whether its caller can tell 'this legitimately found nothing' apart from 'this failed' — if both produce the identical return value, the catch block has deleted information a caller needs, not handled an error.

contentSections.title: What to do with the exception instead

contentSections.body:
The fix isn't removing the try/catch — it's making the catch block do two things a bare `return None` skips: record what actually happened, and give the caller a way to distinguish failure from a legitimate empty result. Recording means logging the exception with enough context to diagnose it later — the exception's type and message, the input that triggered it, ideally a stack trace — not a generic "something went wrong" string that tells a future reader nothing more than the silence would have.

Distinguishing failure from emptiness means the return value (or the function's contract) has to carry that distinction explicitly. A few shapes do this: re-raise a specific, named exception (`DatabaseUnavailableError`) that the caller can catch separately from "no rows found"; return a result type that wraps either a value or an error (`Ok(rows)` / `Err(reason)`, or a tuple `(rows, error)`); or, at minimum, log at the point of failure so the information exists *somewhere*, even if the function's return type stays simple. Which shape fits depends on the language and the codebase's conventions — what doesn't change is the requirement that the information the exception carried has to survive past the point where it's caught, in some form a human or a caller can actually use.

contentSections.scenario: A team adds logging to the original function: `except Exception: logger.error("error"); return None`. Three weeks later, an incident review needs to know how often preference lookups have been failing due to database issues versus genuinely empty results, and can't answer the question from the logs.
contentSections.question: Why does adding this specific log line still leave the team unable to answer the question?

options.label: The log message "error" carries no information about which user_id, which exception type, or what the actual failure was — it's indistinguishable from every other occurrence of the same log line, and can't be correlated with anything
Logging inside a catch block never actually helps with this kind of question, regardless of what's logged
The team should be using a metrics system instead of logs, since logs can never answer aggregate questions

feedback.no-useful-context: Correct. The literal string "error" is logged once per failure with zero distinguishing detail — no exception type, no user_id, no timestamp context beyond whatever the logging framework adds automatically, no indication of whether this was a connection failure, a timeout, or something else entirely. A thousand occurrences of an identical, contentless log line can be counted, but not meaningfully analyzed.
feedback.logging-doesnt-help: Logging is exactly the right instinct — the problem here is specifically what's being logged, not whether logging happens at all. `logger.error('preference lookup failed', extra={'user_id': user_id, 'exception': str(e), 'exception_type': type(e).__name__})` would let this exact question be answered from the same logs.
feedback.should-use-metrics-not-logs: A metrics system is a reasonable *addition* for this kind of aggregate question, and doesn't address why the current logs specifically fail to answer it — the immediate, cheaper fix is putting the actual exception detail into the log line that already exists, which alone would make the question answerable.

contentSections.mechanism: A log line's usefulness during an incident is a direct function of how much it lets someone distinguish this occurrence from every other occurrence of the same code path — a generic message logged identically regardless of cause carries the same amount of information as no log at all, once you already knew the catch block was being hit. The fix isn't logging more often, it's logging the specific, distinguishing facts each time: what failed, for what input, with what underlying error — the exact detail the bare `except Exception: return None` in the original version discarded before anyone could write it down.

contentSections.body: A log line inside a catch block is only as useful as the specific, distinguishing detail it carries — logging the literal word "error" for every possible failure answers no question a future incident review will actually ask.

title: What the caller can actually do about this failure
description: An error message and an exception type that describe what went wrong from the code's own point of view — and give the caller nothing they can act on, because acting on a failure requires knowing which of several very different responses actually applies.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a generated error response gives its caller enough information to choose a correct response — retry, fix input, alert a human, or give up
Distinguish an error that's actionable by its caller from one that only restates that something failed

contentSections.body:
An error's job isn't just to announce that something failed — code doing that much would just as well not have raised at all and let the crash announce it. An error's actual job is to give whatever catches it enough information to choose a correct response, and "correct response" genuinely differs by failure category: a transient failure (a timeout, a 503, a dropped connection) usually warrants a retry; a client-side input problem (invalid address, malformed request) never warrants a retry with the same input and instead needs the input corrected; a configuration or credential problem (expired API key, wrong environment) needs a human, immediately, and retrying just wastes time while the real problem goes unaddressed; a genuine bug in the calling code needs to surface loudly during development, not get quietly retried in production.

Generated code collapses this distinction constantly, because "if not success, raise an exception saying it failed" is a complete, syntactically correct answer to "handle errors from this API call" — and the model has no way to know, from a prompt that doesn't specify it, which of the shipping API's possible failure responses fall into which category. The status code the API actually returned (`400` versus `503` versus `401`) usually contains exactly this distinction already, discarded the moment `response.status_code != 200` collapses every non-200 into one path.

contentSections.scenario: The `create_shipment` function from the hook. The shipping API happens to return `503 Service Unavailable` for a temporary outage, `422 Unprocessable Entity` with a body describing which address field is invalid, and `401 Unauthorized` when the API key has expired — three genuinely different situations that this function's `if response.status_code != 200` collapses into one identical raised exception.
contentSections.question: What's actually lost by collapsing these three status codes into a single generic exception?

options.label: The information the caller would need to choose between retrying, surfacing a validation error to the user, or alerting an operator about credentials — three different, correct responses to three different failures
Nothing meaningful — all three are failures, and the caller just needs to know that the shipment wasn't created, regardless of why
Only some logging detail is lost, which doesn't affect the caller's actual behavior either way

feedback.lost-response-strategy: Correct. A 503 and a 401 both mean 'the shipment wasn't created,' and they call for completely different next actions — retrying a 401 wastes time on a credential problem that a hundred retries won't fix, and not retrying a 503 gives up on a request that would very likely have succeeded thirty seconds later.
feedback.nothing-since-all-failures: This is the assumption baked into the original code, and it's exactly what makes the shipping integration unreliable in practice — 'the shipment wasn't created' is true of all three, but a system that responds to a 503 the same way it responds to a 401 either retries forever against an expired key, or gives up immediately on outages that would have resolved on their own.
feedback.only-logging-detail: This understates it significantly — the caller's actual behavior (whether to retry, whether to alert a human, whether to show the user an error) is exactly what depends on distinguishing these three, not just what ends up in a log line after the fact.

contentSections.concept: The fix preserves the distinction the API already handed over: `if response.status_code == 503: raise TransientShippingError(...)`, `elif response.status_code == 422: raise InvalidShipmentDataError(response.json())`, `elif response.status_code == 401: raise ShippingCredentialsError(...)` — three distinct, named exceptions a caller can catch separately, each implying its own correct response, instead of one generic exception that answers only 'did this fail,' never 'how, and what should happen next.'

contentSections.body: An error's job is to let its caller choose a correct response, and 'retry,' 'fix the input,' and 'alert a human' are genuinely different responses to genuinely different failures — collapsing them into one generic exception discards exactly the information a caller needs to act correctly.

"Actionable" also has to be judged against a specific reader, because an error message useful to one caller can be useless or actively unsafe for a different one. A message meant for a developer reading logs during an incident can and should include internal detail — a stack trace, a query, an internal service name. That same detail, returned directly in an API response shown to an end user, is either confusing (a stack trace means nothing to someone trying to complete a purchase) or a security problem, handing an attacker internal architecture details for free, as covered in an earlier module of this phase.

The practical habit: every error a piece of generated code produces has at least one intended audience, and the useful content differs by audience even when the underlying failure is identical. A caller in application code (another function) needs enough structure to programmatically decide what to do — an exception type or an error code, not prose. A human operator paged at 3am needs the actual failure detail, with enough context to start diagnosing without reproducing the failure first — the subject of the next lesson in this module. An end user needs a plain description of what they can do about it, with none of the internal detail that would help a developer but only clutter or endanger a user-facing response.

contentSections.scenario: The `create_shipment` failure eventually surfaces in three different places: (1) a structured exception caught by the order-processing code that called it, (2) a log line written when that exception is caught, (3) an error banner shown to the customer on the checkout page if shipment creation ultimately fails after retries.
contentSections.question: Select every pairing below where the content is actually appropriate for its audience.

items.label: (1) The exception is a specific, named type (`InvalidShipmentDataError`) carrying the invalid field, not a generic `Exception` with a string message
(2) The log line includes the full stack trace, the order id, and the raw API response body
(3) The customer-facing banner shows the same stack trace and raw API response body that's in the log line
(3) The customer-facing banner says "We couldn't verify your shipping address — please check it and try again"

explanation.exception-typed: This is exactly what the calling code needs to programmatically branch on — a specific exception type is something application code can catch and respond to differently from other failure types, which a generic exception with only a string message can't support.
explanation.log-has-stacktrace: This is exactly the audience that benefits from maximum detail — an engineer diagnosing an incident wants the stack trace, the exact order, and the raw response, and none of that detail is dangerous or confusing when it's sitting in a log system only engineers read.
explanation.user-sees-stacktrace: This is the same detail that was appropriate for the log line, shown to the wrong audience — a customer gets a wall of text they can't act on, and depending on what the stack trace or raw response reveals, potentially internal implementation detail that shouldn't be public at all.
explanation.user-sees-plain-action: This is what a customer actually needs: what's wrong, in plain language, and what they can do about it. It deliberately contains none of the internal detail that made the log line useful — that detail belongs to a different audience.

contentSections.synthesis: The identical underlying failure (an invalid shipping address, rejected by the API) produces three genuinely different messages here, and all three are correct, because each is aimed at what its specific audience actually needs to do next — an application deciding how to branch, an engineer diagnosing an incident, a customer fixing their own input. Writing the same message for all three audiences means it's wrong for at least two of them.

contentSections.body: Ask who actually receives a given error before judging whether its content is right — calling code needs a type it can branch on, an engineer needs full diagnostic detail, and an end user needs a plain description of what they can do, and the same message is rarely correct for more than one of those three.

title: Partial failure: the half-finished write nobody rolls back
description: A multi-step operation where the third of four steps fails, and the first two are left committed — a state nothing in the code anticipated existing, because every code path assumed either all four steps happen or none do.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a multi-step generated operation where a mid-sequence failure leaves earlier steps committed with no rollback or compensating action
Distinguish operations that need true rollback from operations that need a documented, detectable partial state

contentSections.body:
A generated user-signup flow:

```python
def create_account(email, password):
    user = db.users.create(email=email, password_hash=hash_password(password))
    workspace = db.workspaces.create(owner_id=user.id, name=f"{email}'s workspace")
    billing_api.create_customer(email=email, external_id=user.id)
    email_service.send_welcome(email)
    return user
```

Four steps, each depending on the ones before it having succeeded. `billing_api.create_customer` times out because the billing provider is having an incident. The function raises, the signup request fails, and the user sees an error — and the user record and the workspace are both already committed to the database, permanently, because nothing in this function catches the failure and undoes what already happened. The user can't sign up again (the email is taken), can't log in (they never got confirmation the account exists), and support has no visibility into any of this unless someone happens to notice the orphaned row.

This is a distinct failure mode from the transaction-scope gap covered in the previous module of this phase — even a version of this function with every step correctly wrapped in a single database transaction wouldn't fully fix it, because two of the four steps (`billing_api.create_customer`, `email_service.send_welcome`) aren't database operations at all, and no database transaction can roll back a call to an external system that's already succeeded, exactly as that earlier lesson covered. What's specific to *this* lesson is the broader pattern: a sequence of steps, generated as one straight-line function, where the code was written as though the sequence either fully completes or the caller sees an error and nothing happened — with no code path for "steps one and two committed, step three failed, now what."

Generated code produces exactly this straight-line shape because it's the simplest, most literal translation of "create an account, which involves creating a user, a workspace, a billing customer, and sending a welcome email" — four exception-raising calls in a row is a complete, readable answer to that instruction, and nothing about the instruction itself surfaces the question of what happens if step three fails after steps one and two succeeded.

contentSections.code:
def create_account(email, password):
    user = db.users.create(email=email, password_hash=hash_password(password))
    workspace = db.workspaces.create(owner_id=user.id, name=f"{email}'s workspace")
    billing_api.create_customer(email=email, external_id=user.id)
    email_service.send_welcome(email)
    return user
contentSections.question: `billing_api.create_customer` raises a timeout exception. What's the resulting state, precisely?

options.label: The user and workspace rows are already committed to the database and remain there — nothing in this function catches the exception to undo them, so the signup fails from the caller's perspective while two of the four steps have permanently succeeded
Since the function raises an unhandled exception, the runtime automatically rolls back every database write that happened earlier in the same function call
The user record creation itself will also fail, since it depends on the later steps succeeding

feedback.orphaned-user-workspace: Correct. `db.users.create` and `db.workspaces.create` are two separate, already-committed database operations by the time `billing_api.create_customer` even runs — there's no mechanism in this function, and no default behavior in most database clients, that automatically undoes prior committed writes because a later, unrelated statement raised an exception.
feedback.everything-rolled-back: No language or database client provides this behavior by default — an unhandled exception unwinds the call stack and, absent an enclosing transaction that the exception propagates through *before* those writes were committed, has no effect at all on already-committed database rows. This is exactly the assumption that lets this bug ship: it feels like it should be true, and isn't.
feedback.user-record-fails-too: The steps execute strictly in the order written — `db.users.create` completes and returns before `db.workspaces.create` is even called, and both complete before `billing_api.create_customer` is reached. Nothing about a later step failing reaches backward in time to affect a step that already finished.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The function reads as one atomic action — 'create an account' — because it's one function with one name and one return value. Its actual behavior is four independent operations executed in sequence, where the first two are durable and committed well before the third one, the one that actually fails, ever runs. The mismatch between how the function reads (one step) and what it does (four separately-committed steps) is exactly what makes the resulting orphaned state easy to not anticipate.

contentSections.body: A function name describing one action doesn't mean its steps commit together — trace which individual steps are durable and already-committed by the time a later step in the same function can still fail, because that's exactly the state a caller has to be prepared to find.

Not every partial-failure state needs the same fix, and picking the wrong one wastes effort or leaves a real gap. Three genuinely different answers apply depending on what kind of step failed and what's actually recoverable. True rollback — undoing what already happened — works when every step involved is inside a single database transaction; the earlier database-only version of this bug (the transfer-funds example from the previous module) is exactly this case, and the fix there really is widening the transaction's scope. Compensation — running an explicit, separate action that reverses or accounts for a step that already durably happened — is what's needed once an external system is involved and true rollback isn't possible: if `billing_api.create_customer` had succeeded and a *later* step failed, the fix isn't rolling back the billing customer (the billing provider has no concept of this local function's transaction), it's calling `billing_api.delete_customer` explicitly as a compensating action. Detection — accepting that the partial state can occur, and building an explicit way to find and resolve it — is the honest fallback when neither rollback nor a clean compensating action is available: a background job that finds users with no matching billing customer record and either retries the billing call or flags the account for support.

The review question that picks between these three: for each step in a generated multi-step operation, if this step succeeds and a later one fails, is there an explicit action anywhere in the codebase that runs in response — and if not, is the resulting state at least detectable, or does it just silently exist?

contentSections.title: Fixing the create_account partial-failure gap
contentSections.opening: You're reviewing the `create_account` function from this lesson before it ships. You have to decide how to handle the case where `billing_api.create_customer` fails after the user and workspace rows already exist.

n1.situation: You raise the partial-failure gap with the engineer who generated this code. They ask what you'd actually change.
n1.question: What's your first move?

choices.label: Propose wrapping all four steps in a single database transaction so a failure anywhere rolls everything back
choices.consequence: Two of the four steps aren't database operations — a transaction can't roll back an external billing API call or an already-sent email, so this only partially closes the gap and leaves the exact scenario (billing fails after user+workspace commit) just as unrecoverable as before.

choices.label: Ask what should happen, specifically, if billing fails after the user and workspace already exist — retry, compensate, or detect and fix later
choices.consequence: This is the actually productive question — it forces a decision about which of the three strategies fits this specific step, instead of reaching for a generic-sounding fix that doesn't match what actually failed.

n2.situation: The transaction-only fix ships. Three weeks later, a billing provider incident causes several accounts to be created with no billing customer, exactly as before — the transaction boundary never covered the actual failing call.
n2.question: What's the next step?

choices.label: Go back and add the compensation/detection layer that should have been there from the start
choices.consequence: Correct, eventually — but this is the fix that should have shipped the first time, arrived at after a real incident instead of a review comment, which is the more expensive way to learn that a transaction only covers database operations.

n3.situation: The team agrees: retrying billing inline a few times handles transient failures, but a hard failure (the billing provider genuinely rejecting the customer) still needs a fallback.
n3.question: What's the fallback for a hard billing failure, after retries are exhausted?

choices.label: Mark the account 'pending billing setup', let the user proceed with a working account, and run a background job that retries billing creation and alerts support if it keeps failing
choices.consequence: This treats the user and workspace rows as legitimately created (they are) and the billing gap as a separately tracked, detectable, resolvable state — nobody's signup is blocked by a billing provider incident, and nothing about the gap is silent.

choices.label: Delete the user and workspace rows to keep the system 'clean' if billing fails after retries
choices.consequence: This turns a billing provider's problem into the user's problem — their signup silently disappears with no explanation, and if they retry, they may hit a 'workspace name taken' or similar conflict from the deletion not fully cleaning up, which is a worse experience than a working account with a background job resolving billing.

e-good.summary: The account exists and works immediately; the billing gap is tracked, retried automatically, and escalated to a human only if automated retries genuinely can't resolve it.
e-good.lesson: Detection paired with a background resolution path is often the right answer for a step that depends on an external system — it doesn't pretend rollback or inline retry alone will always work, and it doesn't block the user on a dependency that isn't actually required for them to start using the product.

e-costly.summary: The user's signup silently fails after appearing to work, and the cleanup itself can leave the system in a second, different partial state.
e-costly.lesson: Deleting already-committed, legitimate progress to 'undo' an unrelated external failure trades a detectable, resolvable gap for a confusing, user-facing failure — the account holder loses real progress over a billing provider's outage that had nothing to do with them.

e-late.summary: The correct fix eventually ships, after a real incident forced the question the transaction-only fix skipped.
e-late.lesson: A fix that only covers the database half of a multi-system operation looks complete and isn't — the same review question ('what happens to each individual step if a later one fails') would have caught this before shipping instead of after.

contentSections.body: For every step in a generated multi-step operation, ask what happens to it specifically if a later step fails — true rollback only works within a single transaction's reach, an already-succeeded call to an external system needs an explicit compensating action, and where neither is available, the partial state needs to be detectable and resolvable, not silent.

title: Error messages written for the person who'll be paged at 3am
description: The difference between an error message that restates the fact of failure and one that gives a half-asleep on-call engineer, with no memory of this code, enough to start fixing it in under a minute.

learningObjectives.text: Write an error message that includes the specific context (input, state, boundary) needed to diagnose the failure without reproducing it
Identify a generated error message that technically describes the failure while omitting the detail that would make it diagnosable

contentSections.body:
Two versions of the same error, raised from a generated payment-processing function:

```python
# Version A
raise Exception("Payment processing failed")

# Version B
raise PaymentProcessingError(
    f"Charge failed for order {order.id}: provider returned "
    f"'{response.error_code}' ({response.error_message}). "
    f"Amount: {amount} {currency}. Attempt {attempt_number}/{max_attempts}."
)
```

Both are raised from the identical failure. Version A, paged at 3am, tells the engineer exactly one thing: a payment failed, at some point, for some reason, on some order. Every next step — which order, which provider error, whether this is retryable, whether it's one order or a pattern across many — requires them to go dig through code and logs from scratch, awake, at 3am, before they can even start diagnosing the actual problem. Version B answers all of it in the line that paged them.

Generated code defaults toward Version A because a bare `raise Exception("X failed")` is a syntactically complete, technically correct response to "handle this error" — it does communicate that something failed. It's *insufficient*, in the specific sense that matters for an error someone will eventually be paged about: it omits every piece of context that was available at the exact moment of failure and will not be available, or will be much harder to reconstruct, five minutes later during an actual incident.

The context that's cheap to include and expensive to omit is almost always sitting right there in scope at the point the error is raised: the specific identifier involved (which order, which user, which record — not "a" record), the actual values that led to the failure (not just that validation failed, but which field and what it contained), and anything about the failure's shape that changes the response (an error code from a dependency, a retry count, a timestamp). None of this requires new instrumentation or a new system — it requires writing the values that are already local variables in the function into the message, instead of a static string that would read identically whether this is the first occurrence or the thousandth.

contentSections.question: An on-call engineer gets paged with this exception. What's missing that would make it actually diagnosable without reading the source code first?

options.label: Which order this is, what its actual current status is, and why that status blocks a refund — the message states that something is disallowed without saying what makes it disallowed
This shouldn't raise an exception at all — an invalid refund request should just be silently ignored
The real problem is using the built-in `Exception` class instead of a custom one — the message content is otherwise fine

feedback.missing-specifics: Correct. `order.id` and `order.status` are both already local variables at the exact point this exception is raised — including them costs nothing and turns 'cannot process refund' into 'cannot process refund for order 8842: status is pending, not delivered,' which an engineer can act on immediately instead of needing to reproduce the failure to find out what triggered it.
feedback.should-not-raise-at-all: Raising is the right instinct — an invalid refund attempt is a real failure that should stop execution and be visible, not silently ignored, which would hide a genuine problem (a customer trying to refund an order that hasn't shipped, or a bug upstream sending bad requests) behind apparent success.
feedback.needs-different-exception-class: A more specific exception class (something like `InvalidRefundStateError`) is a genuinely good idea for letting callers branch on this failure type, covered in the previous lesson — but it doesn't by itself fix the missing content problem this question is about; a well-named exception class with an equally empty message is still undiagnosable at 3am.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The message states a conclusion ("cannot process refund") without any of the specific facts that led to it, even though both facts — which order, what status — are sitting in local variables at the exact line that raises. The gap isn't a missing investigation; it's a missing two f-string substitutions.

contentSections.body: At the exact point an error is raised, the specific values that caused it are already sitting in scope as local variables — writing them into the message costs nothing and is the single highest-leverage habit for making a generated codebase diagnosable under real incident pressure.

contentSections.title: What belongs in the message, and what doesn't

contentSections.body:
More detail isn't unconditionally better — a message needs the specific facts that explain *this* failure, not everything the function happens to have access to, and the two failure modes on either side of that line are both real. Too little detail is the version this lesson has focused on: "cannot process refund," with the order id and status omitted. Too much detail, in the wrong place, has its own cost: dumping an entire order object, a full request payload including a customer's payment details, or a raw stack trace into a message that ends up in a less-trusted destination (a third-party error-tracking service, a Slack channel with broad membership, a response returned to the client) can leak sensitive data through the exact mechanism meant to help diagnose failures, echoing the error-message leak pattern from the auth-and-secrets module earlier in this phase.

The useful test is specificity, not volume: does this piece of context change what the person reading it would do next? An order id, a status value, a provider error code all pass that test — each one narrows down the cause or points at a next step. A full serialized request object usually doesn't add anything the specific fields didn't already say, while meaningfully raising what's exposed if the message ends up somewhere less trusted than intended.

contentSections.problem: Write a diagnosable error for this failure: a generated inventory-sync job calls `warehouse_api.update_stock(sku, quantity)` for each of 500 SKUs in a nightly batch; SKU 'WBH-2231' fails because the warehouse API returns a 409 conflict (someone else updated this SKU's stock in the warehouse system since this job last read it).

steps.label: Identify the specific, in-scope facts available at the point of failure
steps.work: `sku = 'WBH-2231'`, `quantity` (the value this job tried to write), the HTTP status (409), and the fact that this is one job run out of a 500-SKU batch — is it the only failure, or one of several?
steps.why: These are the facts that actually distinguish this failure from every other possible failure in this same function, and every one of them is already available without any extra work.

steps.label: Choose a specific exception type reflecting the failure category
steps.work: A 409 conflict is neither 'retry blindly' nor 'a code bug' — it's a genuine concurrent-modification conflict, closer to the read-then-write race pattern from the concurrency module. `StockSyncConflictError` communicates that category directly.
steps.why: The exception type itself is the first piece of diagnostic information an on-call engineer sees, often before they even read the message — a specific type narrows the search before any prose does.

steps.label: Write the message with the specific facts substituted in
steps.work: `raise StockSyncConflictError(f"Stock sync conflict for SKU {sku}: warehouse API returned 409 (external update since last read). Attempted quantity: {quantity}. Batch: {batch_id}, item {index+1}/{total}.")`
steps.why: This message alone tells the engineer which SKU, why it's a conflict rather than an outage, what was attempted, and whether to expect this to be isolated or part of a larger pattern in this batch — enough to decide 'skip and re-sync this SKU next run' without opening a debugger.

faded.problem: The same batch job also fails on SKU 'GRD-0087', but this time because `warehouse_api.update_stock` times out after 10 seconds with no response at all — a transient network issue, not a conflict.

blanks.prompt: What exception type fits this failure category, distinct from the conflict case?
blanks.answer: StockSyncTimeoutError (or an equivalent name specifically distinguishing a transient/retryable failure from the conflict case)
accept: a timeout-specific or transient-failure exception type, distinct from StockSyncConflictError
blanks.why: A timeout is retryable in a way a 409 conflict isn't — collapsing both into the same exception type would lose exactly the distinction the previous lesson covered, between failures that warrant a retry and failures that don't.

blanks.prompt: What specific facts belong in this message, beyond the SKU and the exception type?
blanks.answer: The quantity attempted, the timeout duration, and the batch/item position (e.g. batch_id, index+1/total) — the same shape of context as the conflict case, substituted for this failure's actual facts
accept: quantity, timeout length, and batch position, matching the level of detail in the worked conflict example
blanks.why: The specific facts differ (a timeout duration instead of a conflict reason), but the standard — enough detail to act without reproducing the failure — is identical across both failure types, which is the actual generalizable habit this lesson is teaching.

faded.procedure: For any error raised in generated code: name the failure category with a specific exception type, then substitute every already-in-scope fact that would change what the reader does next directly into the message — never a generic string that would read identically regardless of which specific failure actually occurred.

contentSections.body: Test every piece of context before adding it to an error message with one question: would this change what the reader does next? That standard adds the order id and the status value, and leaves out the full serialized object that just repeats what the specific fields already said while exposing more than necessary.

title: Timeouts, retries and backoff that don't make things worse
description: A generated retry loop that fires again the instant a call fails, with no delay and no cap — correct in isolation, and the exact mechanism that turns a struggling dependency into a fully downed one.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a generated retry implementation with no backoff or cap as a mechanism that can worsen an outage rather than recover from it
Explain how exponential backoff and jitter reduce the load a retry storm places on an already-struggling dependency

contentSections.title: The retry that makes the outage worse

contentSections.body:
A retry loop with no delay between attempts is correct for exactly one failure mode — a single, isolated, already-resolved blip — and actively harmful for the much more common one: a dependency that's degraded under load, where an instant retry adds to the exact load causing the degradation. "Retry on failure" is a complete, reasonable-sounding answer to "make this call more resilient," and it's also the shape generated code reaches for by default, because the *rate* at which retries happen isn't part of the literal instruction — nothing about "retry a few times" specifies how much time to leave between attempts, so a model filling in that gap has no signal pointing it toward the pause that turns out to matter most.

This compounds across a real system rather than staying isolated: if a hundred different callers all hold references to the same struggling downstream service, and all of them are running this same no-delay retry pattern, a single service degradation multiplies into a synchronized retry storm — every caller's tenth attempt landing in the same narrow window as every other caller's tenth attempt, which is the opposite of resilience. This has a name in distributed-systems practice: a retry storm, and it's a well-documented way an initially minor, recoverable slowdown becomes a full outage.

contentSections.scenario: A payments service starts timing out on roughly 30% of requests due to a database performance issue — not down, genuinely still processing most requests correctly, just slower than usual. Every service calling it uses the `call_with_retry` wrapper from the hook. Within two minutes of the slowdown starting, the payments service becomes completely unresponsive to all requests.
contentSections.question: What's the mechanism connecting a 30% partial slowdown to a complete outage two minutes later?

options.label: Every timed-out request is immediately retried up to ten times with no delay, so the 30% of requests that were merely slow generate a much larger multiple of that volume in near-instant repeat requests, pushing total load well past what the already-struggling service can handle
This pattern strongly suggests a second, unrelated incident occurred at almost the same time as the database slowdown
A 30% failure rate on a database issue commonly cascades into complete failure on its own, regardless of retry behavior

feedback.retry-amplification: Correct. Each of the original 30% of slow requests can generate up to ten near-instant retries from the calling side — call volume against the struggling service doesn't stay at 130% of normal, it can spike many times higher, entirely driven by retry behavior rather than by any change in the underlying database issue, which is precisely the mechanism that turns a partial slowdown into a total outage on a compressed timeline.
feedback.unrelated-second-incident: Nothing about this timeline requires a second cause — the retry-amplification mechanism alone, acting on the original single database issue, is sufficient to explain the total outage that follows, without needing to invoke an unrelated coincidental event.
feedback.database-issue-alone: A struggling-but-functional database serving 70% of requests successfully doesn't inherently escalate to zero on its own within minutes — that specific, rapid collapse is the signature of an external amplifying factor, and the no-delay retry wrapper calling this service from every direction is exactly that factor.

contentSections.mechanism: A retry without a delay treats every failure as independent and isolated, when in a real system many failures share a common cause — a struggling dependency — and are not independent at all. Retrying that shared cause immediately and repeatedly doesn't address the actual bottleneck (database performance); it adds directly to the load causing it, at the worst possible moment, from every caller simultaneously. The fix has to change the *rate* of retries, not just their count: a growing delay between attempts (exponential backoff) gives a struggling dependency room to recover instead of drowning it in synchronized immediate retries.

contentSections.body: A retry loop with no delay between attempts assumes every failure is an isolated, already-resolved blip — against a dependency that's degraded under load, the same retry behavior adds directly to the load causing the degradation, and can turn a partial slowdown into a total outage.

contentSections.title: Backoff, jitter, and a cap that actually stops

contentSections.body:
Exponential backoff fixes the rate problem by growing the delay between attempts — a common shape is `delay = base_delay * (2 ** attempt_number)`, so attempt one waits roughly a second, attempt two waits two seconds, attempt three waits four, and so on, giving a struggling dependency progressively more room to recover instead of a constant hammering. On its own, though, exponential backoff has a subtler problem: if every caller started retrying at the exact same moment (because they all received their original failure at the same moment, from the same shared outage), pure exponential backoff keeps their retries synchronized too — attempt three from every caller still lands in the same narrow window, just a less frequent one. Jitter — adding a small random offset to each computed delay — breaks that synchronization, spreading a thundering herd of simultaneous retries into a smoother, staggered trickle the dependency can actually absorb.

A retry loop also needs a real cap, and "stop after N attempts" alone isn't quite that cap — the code has to define, and act on, what happens when N attempts are all exhausted. `raise Exception("All retries failed")`, from the hook's original version, at least surfaces the exhaustion rather than looping forever, but per the earlier lessons in this module, it also needs to be a specific, diagnosable error — which failure, which attempt, what the last underlying error actually was — not a generic string that tells whoever catches it nothing beyond "this eventually gave up."

contentSections.scenario: A retry uses exponential backoff with `base_delay = 1` second and the formula `delay = base_delay * (2 ** attempt_number)`, for attempt numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 (four attempts total, the delay applied before each retry after the first failed attempt).
contentSections.question: Predict the delay, in seconds, before the fourth attempt (attempt_number = 3) — i.e., roughly how long has this caller been retrying by the time it makes its final attempt, just from this one delay?
contentSections.explanation: `1 * (2 ** 3) = 8` seconds before the fourth attempt alone — on top of the 1, 2, and 4 second delays before attempts two and three, the caller has already waited 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 seconds before this final 8-second wait even begins, for roughly 15 seconds of total backoff across four attempts. This is exactly the growth pattern that gives a struggling dependency meaningfully more breathing room with each successive attempt, compared to a flat, repeated 1-second (or zero-second) delay that never increases no matter how many times the same caller has already failed.

contentSections.body: A resilient retry needs three things together, not any one alone: a growing delay between attempts (backoff) so retries ease off rather than hammering a struggling dependency, randomness in that delay (jitter) so many callers' retries don't stay synchronized, and a real cap whose exhaustion raises a specific, diagnosable error instead of looping forever or failing silently.

title: Rebuild the failure handling of a generated integration
description: Take a generated integration with an external service, and rebuild its failure handling end to end — what breaks, what the user sees, and what the log says — instead of patching one swallowed exception at a time.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's diagnosability, actionability, and partial-failure checks to a genuinely AI-generated integration, not a curated example
Produce a failure table mapping each failure mode of a real integration to its user-facing behavior and its log output

contentSections.body: Every broken error path this module used already had its defect flagged for you. A real integration doesn't come with its failure modes labeled — it comes as code that works when the dependency is healthy, and the only way to find out how it actually fails is to go looking, deliberately, for every place it can. This lab is that search, against a real generated integration, end to end.

contentSections.title: Rebuild the failure handling of a generated integration
contentSections.brief: Pick a small integration with an external service you'd genuinely want built — sending email through a provider's API, calling a payment or shipping API, syncing data to a third-party service, calling an LLM API. Generate real code for it from an AI tool, including whatever error handling it produces by default. Find every distinct way this integration can fail — the dependency times out, returns an error status, returns malformed data, is misconfigured, rejects the input — and rebuild the failure handling for each one against this module's standards: no swallowed errors, an actionable, specific error for each failure category, explicit handling for any partial-failure state, and safe retry behavior where retries apply.
contentSections.deliverable: The rebuilt integration code, plus a failure table with one row per failure mode: what breaks, what the user sees, and what the log says.

stages.title: Generate and enumerate failure modes
stages.instructions: Generate the integration. List every distinct way it can fail — not just 'the API call fails' as one entry, but each genuinely different cause (timeout, 4xx client error, 5xx server error, malformed response, auth failure, rate limit) as its own row.
stages.checkpoint: A list of distinct failure modes exists, each one a genuinely different cause rather than a restatement of 'something failed.'

stages.title: Audit the generated error handling against each mode
stages.instructions: For each failure mode from stage 1, trace what the generated code currently does: does it swallow the error, raise something generic, raise something specific and actionable, or handle it correctly already? Flag every mode where the current handling loses information a caller or an on-call engineer would need.
stages.checkpoint: Every failure mode has a documented current behavior, and every gap is flagged with what specifically is missing.

stages.title: Rebuild the handling and check partial failure
stages.instructions: Rewrite the error handling for each flagged gap: specific exception types, diagnosable messages with in-scope context, and — if this integration is one step in a larger operation — explicit handling for what happens to earlier, already-committed steps if this integration's call fails partway through. If retries apply, confirm backoff and a real cap are in place.
stages.checkpoint: Every flagged gap has a concrete fix in the rewritten code, and partial-failure and retry behavior have both been explicitly considered, even if the answer for one of them is 'not applicable here, because...'

stages.title: Write the failure table and self-check
stages.instructions: Compress the result into the deliverable's failure table: one row per failure mode, with what breaks, what the user sees, and what the log says. Self-check against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: The failure table covers every mode from stage 1, and every row states real, specific content for both the user-facing and the log-facing columns.

rubric.criterion: Every distinct failure mode of the real integration is enumerated, not just a generic 'API call fails' case
rubric.meets: The failure table has a genuinely separate row for each cause (timeout, 4xx, 5xx, malformed response, auth failure, and any others specific to this integration) rather than one row covering all of them.

rubric.criterion: Each failure mode's log-facing content is specific enough to diagnose without reproducing the failure
rubric.meets: Each row's log content includes the concrete, in-scope facts this module's lessons called for — not a generic string that would read identically for every failure mode.

rubric.criterion: Each failure mode's user-facing content is appropriate for its audience
rubric.meets: The user-facing column states what an end user would actually see, containing no internal detail (stack traces, raw API responses) that belongs in the log column instead.

rubric.criterion: Partial-failure and retry behavior are explicitly addressed
rubric.meets: If this integration is one step among others, the deliverable states what happens to earlier steps if this one fails partway through; if retries apply, backoff, jitter, and a cap are all present and reasoned about, not just a raw attempt count.

rubric.criterion: The rebuilt code and failure table are usable as a real review artefact going forward
rubric.meets: Someone other than you could read the failure table and understand exactly how this integration behaves under each failure mode, without this module's lessons open beside it.

contentSections.body: A failure table built from a real integration's actual failure modes is worth more than a general error-handling checklist — it forces every abstract standard from this module (diagnosable, actionable, safe to retry) to answer a concrete question about one specific piece of code you generated yourself.

title: Checkpoint — Error Handling and Failure Paths
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Concurrency, Time and Ordering, two from further back in this phase. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's swallowed-error, actionable-error, partial-failure, diagnosability, and retry-safety patterns alongside earlier modules' concurrency and authorization patterns, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Error Handling and Failure Paths

questions.from: This module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A function's `except Exception: return None` returns the identical value whether the query found no rows or the database was unreachable. What's the actual defect?

options.label: The caller cannot distinguish 'legitimately found nothing' from 'the lookup failed' — both produce the same return value, and a real failure reads as normal, empty behavior
The function should use async database calls instead of synchronous ones
The try/catch block itself shouldn't exist at all

questions.explanation: Collapsing every possible failure into the same value as a legitimate empty result deletes the information a caller needs — the fix is a specific exception, a result type, or at minimum a log line with the actual failure detail, not removing error handling.

questions.from: This module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A generated shipping API client raises the identical generic exception whether the API is down (503), the address is invalid (422), or the API key expired (401). What's lost?

options.label: The information the caller needs to choose between retrying, surfacing a validation error, or alerting an operator — three different correct responses to three different failures
Nothing meaningful, since all three genuinely mean the shipment wasn't created
Only some logging detail, which doesn't affect the caller's actual behavior

questions.explanation: A 503 and a 401 both mean 'not created' and call for opposite responses — retrying a 401 wastes time on a credential problem, and not retrying a 503 gives up on a request likely to succeed shortly after.

questions.from: This module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A generated `create_account` function creates a user row, then a workspace row, then calls a billing API that fails. What's the resulting state?

options.label: The user and workspace rows are already committed and remain in the database — nothing automatically undoes them because a later, unrelated call failed
The runtime automatically rolls back the earlier database writes since the function raised an unhandled exception
The user row creation fails too, since it depends on the later steps succeeding

questions.explanation: Steps execute and commit in order; nothing about a later failure reaches backward to undo an earlier, already-committed step, unless the code explicitly wraps them in a shared transaction or adds a compensating action.

questions.from: This module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A retry loop with no delay between attempts hits a downstream service that's degraded (not down) under load. What's the mechanism by which this can turn a partial slowdown into a total outage?

options.label: Every timed-out request is immediately retried multiple times with no delay, multiplying load against the already-struggling service well past what it can handle
This pattern typically indicates a second, unrelated incident happening at the same time
A partial slowdown on its own commonly escalates to total failure regardless of retry behavior

questions.explanation: Retry-amplification adds directly to the load causing the original degradation, from every caller simultaneously — the fix is exponential backoff with jitter, so retries ease off instead of compounding the problem.

questions.from: Previous module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: Two requests both call a `purchase()` function that reads stock, checks it, then writes a decremented value back, against a product with 1 unit left. Why can both requests succeed under the default relational isolation level?

options.label: Both requests can read the same pre-write stock value before either one's write lands, so both pass the check based on the same now-stale snapshot
The `>=` comparison operator is incorrect and should be `>`
This can only happen if the database has no transaction support at all

questions.explanation: The read, check, and write are separate operations with no guarantee nothing else touches the row between them — the fix is an atomic conditional UPDATE or explicit row lock, not a different operator.

questions.from: Previous module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: A payment request times out because the response was delayed, not because the charge failed, and the client retries with no idempotency key. What does the client actually know about whether the first charge succeeded?

options.label: Nothing — a timeout is consistent with the charge having failed, succeeded, or still being processed
It knows the charge failed, since a successful charge would have returned before timing out
It knows the charge succeeded, since most timeouts happen after processing completes

questions.explanation: A timeout is defined by the absence of a response in time, consistent with several server-side outcomes — the fix is an idempotency key generated before the first attempt.

questions.from: Previous module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: A generated `transfer(from_id, to_id, amount)` function wraps only the debit inside `with db.transaction():`, with the credit running as separate calls after the block closes. What's the precise defect?

options.label: Everything after the transaction block's closing line is outside it and gets none of its guarantees, regardless of how naturally it reads as part of the same operation
The debit and credit are performed in the wrong logical order
The function is missing input validation on `amount`

questions.explanation: A transaction only covers what's lexically inside its boundary — proximity or apparent intent doesn't extend it.

questions.from: Previous module — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: A generated 'is this the user's birthday today' check uses `datetime.now()` on the server. Why does this pass every local test while still being wrong for users in other timezones?

options.label: The test and the code share the same implicit assumption — both resolve 'today' in the developer's own timezone, so they always agree with each other regardless of whether that's correct for a real user elsewhere
The tests don't cover enough different birthdate values
This bug is rare enough that testing wouldn't reasonably catch it

questions.explanation: A test's blind spot is often structurally identical to the code's blind spot, because both share the same implicit timezone assumption.

questions.from: Two modules back — Auth, Secrets and Permissions
questions.prompt: `requireAuth` middleware confirms a request carries a valid session. What question does it leave completely unanswered?

options.label: Whether this specific identity is allowed to do this specific thing to this specific resource
Whether the request came over HTTPS
Whether the session token is well-formed

questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity and stops there — authorization is a separate check that has to be written explicitly.

questions.from: Three modules back — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated checkout function has zero conditionals and operates on a list of cart items. What should that absence of branching make you check first?

options.label: What happens when the list is empty — the single most common non-happy-path state a function meets
Whether the function's variable names are descriptive enough
Whether the function runs fast enough for a large cart

questions.explanation: Zero conditionals in an edge-case-heavy domain is the structural tell for happy-path-only code, and an empty collection is usually the single most common non-happy-path input a function actually meets.
